Abstract

Earthquake Early Warning Systems (EEWS) are designed to provide alerts before the most damaging seismic waves of an earthquake reach populated areas, giving people precious seconds to take protective actions. However, traditional EEWS rely heavily on dense seismic networks and often face challenges in rapidly detecting earthquakes in regions with limited infrastructure or fewer stations. In response to these limitations, and in order to provide faster warning even in well-instrumented areas, we design an AI-based algorithm, coined E3WS for Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System, which detects earthquakes and estimate their magnitude and location using 3 seconds of data recorded on a single station. This design not only improves the time response but also enables E3WS to operate effectively in areas with fewer stations, making it a flexible solution that can be applied not only in the studied regions but also globally, enhancing early warning capabilities in diverse tectonic settings. We install E3WS as the core algorithm of the Peruvian EEWS (SASPe for Sistema de Alerta Sísmica Perúano), providing timely alerts for subduction earthquakes along the coast and benefiting more than 18 million Peruvians. SASPe operates through a network of 111 stations, where E3WS is independently implemented. Beyond Peru, we use E3WS to forecast aftershocks in Haiti, to detect seismic swarms in Ecuador, and to study a foreshock sequence leading up to a major earthquake that occurred in Arequipa, Peru.

Keywords : Earthquakes, Early Warning, Artificial intelligence.

Résumé

Les systèmes d'alerte précoce des tremblements de terre (EEWS) sont conçus pour fournir des alertes avant que les ondes sismiques les plus destructrices d'un séisme n'atteignent les zones peuplées, offrant ainsi quelques précieuses secondes aux populations pour prendre des mesures de protection. Cependant, les EEWS traditionnels dépendent fortement de réseaux sismiques denses et rencontrent souvent des difficultés à détecter rapidement les séismes dans les régions disposant d'une infrastructure limitée ou de moins de stations. En réponse à ces limitations, et afin de fournir des alertes plus rapides même dans les zones bien équipées, nous avons conçu un algorithme basé sur l'intelligence artificielle, nommé E3WS (Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System), qui détecte les tremblements de terre et estime leur magnitude et leur localisation en utilisant 3 secondes de données enregistrées sur une seule station. Ce concept permet non seulement d'améliorer le temps de réponse, mais aussi de faire fonctionner E3WS de manière efficace dans des zones disposant de moins de stations, en faisant une solution flexible pouvant être appliquée non seulement dans les régions étudiées, mais également à l'échelle mondiale, renforçant ainsi les capacités d'alerte précoce dans des contextes tectoniques divers. Nous avons installé E3WS comme algorithme central du système d'alerte précoce sismique péruvien (SASPe pour Sistema de Alerta Sísmica Peruano), fournissant des alertes précoces pour les séismes de subduction le long de la côte et bénéficiant à plus de 18 millions de Péruviens. SASPe fonctionne à travers un réseau de 111 stations, où E3WS est implémenté de manière indépendante. Au-delà du Pérou, nous utilisons E3WS pour prévoir les répliques en Haïti, détecter les essaims sismiques en Équateur, et étudier une séquence de séismes précurseurs précédant un séisme majeur survenu à Arequipa, au Pérou.

Mots-clés : Tremblements de terre, Alerte précoce, Intelligence artificielle.

General Introduction

Earthquakes are among the most unpredictable and destructive natural disasters, posing a significant threat to human life and infrastructure. Over the past decades, several major earthquakes have resulted in substantial loss of life and extensive damage. For instance, the 2010 Haiti earthquake, with a moment magnitude (Mw) of 7.0, caused around 300,000 deaths and left 1.5 million people homeless. Similarly, the 2011 Tohoku earthquake in Japan, which had a Mw of 9.1, led to around 15,641 deaths and caused $211 billion in damages, making it the costliest natural disaster in history. These events highlight the critical need for effective and timely earthquake detection and response systems.

Earthquake Early Warning Systems (EEWS) are designed to detect the initial, less-destructive P-waves of an earthquake and provide alerts before the more destructive S-waves arrive. The development of these systems has proven to be a vital tool in reducing the impact of earthquakes by allowing individuals and automated systems to take precautionary actions. EEWS provide critical seconds of warning, giving people the opportunity to take protective measures and enabling automated systems, such as shutting down trains and industrial machinery, to prevent further damage.

Countries such as Japan, Mexico, and the United States have implemented sophisticated EEWS that send public alerts to populations in seismically active regions. Japan's EEWS, for example, has been instrumental in minimizing the impact of earthquakes by providing early warnings through mobile phones, television, and radio broadcasts. Similarly, Mexico's Sistema de Alerta Sísmico Mexicano (SASMEX) has been alerting the public to seismic threats since 1993, significantly reducing casualties in urban areas. However, while these systems are effective, their performance depends on the density and coverage of seismic networks, and the accuracy and speed of the underlying algorithms used to process seismic data.

Traditional earthquake detection methods rely heavily on networks of seismometers and algorithms such as the Short-Term Average/Long-Term Average (STA/LTA) method, which is used to detect seismic activity by identifying sudden increases in signal amplitude. While these methods have been successful, they face several limitations. For instance, sparse seismic networks in certain regions delay detection times, and algorithms such as STA/LTA can struggle in environments with low signal-to-noise ratios, leading to false positives or missed events. These issues highlight the need for improved detection technologies that can provide faster and more accurate warnings.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a transformative tool in seismology, offering new methods to enhance the detection and characterization of seismic events. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms are particularly well-suited for analyzing large datasets, identifying patterns, and making rapid decisions without the need for extensive manual intervention. These techniques have already been applied in a variety of fields, including healthcare and astrophysics, and their potential in seismology is becoming increasingly evident. In particular, AI models are capable of automating the detection of earthquakes, estimating their magnitudes, and providing timely alerts based on real-time data.

AI models have several advantages over traditional methods. Deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are capable of automatically extracting meaningful features from raw seismic data, reducing the need for manual feature engineering. These models can process continuous seismic waveforms, detect microseismicity, and identify patterns that may be difficult to discern using traditional methods.

Traditional machine learning models, such as XGBoost (XGB), offer a balance between accuracy, speed, and computational efficiency, making them ideal for real-time earthquake detection. A key advantage of these models is that they can be installed on simpler, lower-cost devices, such as Raspberry Pi, enabling their deployment in regions with limited infrastructure or directly onsite. This on-site processing approach significantly reduces the need for transmitting large amounts of seismic data in real time. For instance, in an Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) context, only small-sized warning information, such as estimated magnitude and location, needs to be transferred to the warning center rather than the entire waveform data. This makes the communication lighter, faster, and more robust, ensuring that critical alerts can be transmitted swiftly while minimizing bandwidth and reducing potential delays. Such efficiency is crucial in delivering timely warnings to vulnerable populations.

The integration of machine learning into earthquake detection reflects the ongoing need for faster and more reliable EEWS, especially in areas where infrastructure is limited, or people live in close proximity to seismic sources. Machine learning has emerged as a transformative tool in seismology, capable of enhancing the accuracy and speed of detection, as well as supporting new applications such as real-time magnitude estimation and source characterization. These advancements have the potential to significantly improve the effectiveness of EEWS, ensuring that alerts are delivered more quickly and accurately to populations at risk, allowing for better preparation and mitigation of earthquake impacts.

Research Objectives and Thesis Structure

The goal of this thesis is to design and apply in a real-world context an ensemble machine learning algorithm based on a single station that functions as a complete EEWS package, capable of earthquake detection and source characterization estimates. The system should be compatible with both high-end and low-end sensors, allowing it to serve as both an EEWS and a tool for traditional tasks such as catalog generation (earthquake detection), P-phase arrival estimation, magnitude estimation, and determining epicentral distance, back-azimuth and hypocentral

depth. Moreover, the algorithm should provide physical insights by exploring machine learning attributes (feature importance) that reveal deeper aspects of seismology.

This research seeks to bridge the gap between conventional seismological techniques and AI, offering a new paradigm for seismic hazard mitigation.

This thesis is organized into the following chapters:

- -Chapter I: Earthquake Early Warning: challenges and perspective - This chapter describes a broad overview of the seismic risks faced by human societies and the urgent need for enhanced detection systems. It begins by discussing the unpredictable nature of earthquakes and the crucial role of EEWS in reducing their impact. The chapter highlights the limitations of traditional seismological signal detection, especially in regions with sparse seismic networks, and the challenges posed by noisy environments. A key focus is placed on the development of scalable, single-station algorithms as a solution to these limitations. By leveraging Artificial Intelligence, single-station approaches can offer real-time earthquake detection and source characterization without the need for large sensor networks. The chapter emphasizes how these AI-driven models, particularly traditional ML algorithms such as XGBoost (XGB), can be deployed in cost-effective, on-site systems to deliver rapid and reliable earthquake warnings, even in areas with limited infrastructure, setting the stage for the thesis's focus on advancing EEWS through single-station AI algorithms.
- -Chapter II: Earthquake Early Warning Starting From 3 s of Records on a Single Station With Machine Learning - This chapter provides a detailed description of the Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System (E3WS), an EEWS that starts from 3 seconds of records on a single station, leveraging machine learning algorithms (Lara et al., 2023). It covers the system's design, which integrates detection, P-phase picking, and source characterization for magnitude, epicentral distance, depth, and back-azimuth estimation. The chapter also discusses the versatility and scalability of E3WS, along with its application to both minor and major earthquakes worldwide. Moreover, it presents a comparison with other EEWS systems, evaluating its performance and highlighting the feasibility of installing E3WS on low-cost devices, such as Raspberry Pi. It describes the system's infrastructure, consisting of 111 strong-motion stations equipped with three-component accelerometers and low-cost processors, such as Raspberry Pi 4, enabling efficient on-site data processing. This chapter also presents real-time case studies of major earthquakes, demonstrating SASPe's performance and early warning capabilities. regions, demonstrating its versatility in aftershock forecasting, foreshock analysis, and seismic swarm detection. 1.1 The earthquake threat and the benefit of early detection

Natural disasters have long posed significant threats to human societies, with earthquakes standing out as one of the most unpredictable and destructive forces of nature. Over the past two decades, earthquakes have resulted in substantial loss of life and displacement of millions. For instance, the 2010 Haiti earthquake, which struck with a moment magnitude (Mw) of 7.0, caused approximately 300,000 deaths and left 1.5 million people homeless (DesRoches et al., 2011). Economically, the consequences can be equally devastating. The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and subsequent tsunami in Japan, which resulted in the deaths of around 15,641 people (Mori et al., 2011), caused an estimated $211 billion in damages, making it the costliest natural disaster in recorded history (Kajitani et al., 2013).

According to the NCEI/WDS Global Significant Earthquake Database 1 , since 2000, an average of 35,568 people died annually from earthquakes, with economic losses averaging $77,191 million per year (Figure 1.1). The sharp contrast between the 2010 Mw 7.0 Haiti earthquake and the 2011 Mw 9.1 Tohoku earthquake highlights the crucial role of early earthquake detection. Despite the Tohoku earthquake's larger magnitude, its offshore location and Japan's advanced Earthquake Early Warning System (EEWS) helped mitigate the death toll, as many fatalities were caused by the tsunami rather than the earthquake itself. Japan's EEWS provided residents with precious seconds to brace for impact, automatically halting trains and issuing alerts through mobile and broadcast systems. In contrast, the 2004 Mw 9.1 Sumatra earthquake, which triggered the devastating Indian Ocean tsunami and caused over 283,000 deaths, saw catastrophic losses across several countries due to the absence of a regional EEWS (Lay et al., 2005). The absence of an EEWS left the population completely unprepared, reflecting the critical importance of rapid earthquake detection and early warning systems in saving lives, especially in densely populated or high-risk areas.

Moreover, the economic impact of earthquakes extends far beyond the immediate cost of damaged infrastructure. These disasters can disrupt entire economies, leading to long-term financial losses that hinder development, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. For instance, the twin earthquakes in Turkey on February 6, 2023, with Mw of 7.8 and 7.6, caused over 45,000 deaths (Dal Zilio and Ampuero, 2023) and an estimated $34.2 billion in infrastructure damage, equivalent to 4% of the country's 2021 Gross Domestic Product (GDP). However, the total recovery cost is likely to be even higher due to the broader economic disruptions that follow such events (Kahraman, 2023). The aftermath of these disasters places significant strain on national resources, diverting funds from essential services like education and healthcare, and further exacerbating poverty and inequality.

Effective detection can play a crucial role in minimizing the economic and infrastructural damage that often accompanies these disasters. According to the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), earthquakes events have been responsible for 58% of all deaths (721,318) caused by natural disasters over the past two decades (Figure 1.2), highlighting the deadly nature of these events and the urgent need for reliable detection and warning systems (Van Loenhout et al., 2020).

Recognizing the importance of earthquake detection, the international community has emphasized it as a crucial element of disaster risk management strategies. The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, adopted by the United Nations in 2015, underscores the need for enhanced monitoring and early warning systems to reduce disaster risk and strengthen resilience (Pearson and Pelling, 2015). This global commitment reflects the understanding that early detection and warning are key to minimizing the impacts of earthquakes and ensuring that communities are better prepared to respond and recover.

The functionality of an EEWS consists of detecting the initial seismic waves (P-waves) and issuing real-time alerts, estimating the earthquake's location, magnitude, and potential impact before the more destructive secondary waves (S-waves) arrive (Figure 1.3). Typically, these alerts are issued based on an alert radius determined by the estimate of Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) or Peak Ground Velocity (PGV) thresholds (Zollo et al., 2009). These systems provide crucial seconds to minutes for individuals and automated systems to respond, prompting protective actions like the 'Drop, Cover, and Hold On', which has been shown to reduce injuries and fatalities (Burkett et al., 2014). Automated responses, such as halting trains, shutting down power plants, and activating emergency services, further prevent damage. By leveraging the near-instantaneous speed of light communication, EEWS transmit warnings faster than seismic waves travel, allowing alerts to reach affected populations before the arrival of the more destructive S-waves and surface waves. This brief but critical window of warning plays a key role in saving lives, reducing economic losses, and enhancing the resilience of critical infrastructure. Expanding and improving EEWS, especially in seismically vulnerable regions, is crucial for effective disaster preparedness and response.

Moreover, as the global population grows and urbanization increases in seismically active regions, the need for robust earthquake detection systems becomes even more urgent. Investing in and advancing these systems is not only essential for public safety but also a crucial aspect of sustainable development and resilience building in the face of natural disasters. Countries such as Japan, Mexico, and the United States implemented sophisticated EEWS, often utilizing multiple algorithms, which send public alerts and are integrated into national disaster response frameworks, helping to mitigate the impacts of earthquakes on both lives and infrastructure.

Despite the advancements in EEWS, their effectiveness hinges on several critical factors, particularly the accurate and timely detection of seismological signals. A balance must be struck between issuing the fastest alert and providing the most accurate one (Meier, 2017), as longer analysis time leads to more accurate estimates, but it reduces the user lead time. Furthermore, the density and coverage of the seismic network are critical to detecting earthquakes as quickly as possible, as having sensors close to the epicenter significantly reduces detection time. Implementing an effective EEWS not only requires a thorough understanding of the region's seismology but also demands a sufficient number of stations to ensure comprehensive coverage. The speed of data processing is equally vital, as it determines how quickly a system can issue a warning after detecting the initial seismic signals. Additionally, public awareness and preparedness are essential to ensure that warnings are effectively acted upon.

Studies have shown that individuals who are informed about how to respond to earthquake alerts are significantly more likely to take protective actions, such as the 'Drop, Cover, and Hold On', which can reduce injuries and fatalities during seismic events (Arlikatti et al., 2019). However, preparedness goes beyond awareness; regular drills and educational campaigns are crucial for ensuring the public knows how to react when a warning is issued. For example, in Japan, disaster prevention education and frequent tsunami evacuation drills have significantly increased preparedness, particularly in schools, where students' awareness and response times have proven vital during events like the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake (León et al., 2021). In contrast, regions lacking such preparedness measures may see less effective responses, diminishing the potential life-saving benefits of the system. Thus, a well-established EEWS must be accompanied by public education and preparedness initiatives to maximize its impact.

In regions with limited resources, the implementation of robust EEWS presents significant challenges. These areas often lack the dense seismic instrumentation needed for comprehensive signal detection, which can result in delayed or less accurate warnings. Therefore, there is a pressing need to develop cost-effective and accessible technologies that can reliably detect seismological signals and provide timely warnings, even in regions with sparse seismic networks. Advancements in the detection of these signals are paramount to expanding the reach and effectiveness of EEWS, ensuring that even the most vulnerable populations are protected from the devastating impacts of earthquakes.

Beyond their critical role in EEWS, the accurate detection of seismological signals is fundamental to advancing our understanding of earthquake physics. By capturing and analyzing these signals, researchers can generate detailed earthquake catalogs, which are essential for studying the behavior and characteristics of seismic events. These catalogs provide invaluable data on the frequency, magnitude, and distribution of earthquakes, serving as the foundation for various models that predict seismic hazards and inform building codes and land-use planning.

Accurate earthquake catalogs also enable the identification of foreshocks, aftershocks, and the patterns of seismic activity that precede major earthquakes, offering insights into the underlying mechanisms of fault movement and stress accumulation. This knowledge is crucial for improving seismic hazard assessments and for refining the algorithms used in EEWS, leading to more reliable and timely warnings. Furthermore, by understanding the physics of earthquakes more thoroughly, scientists can enhance the resilience of communities by developing strategies that mitigate the risks associated with future seismic events.

As we continue to harness the benefits of seismological signal detection for both EEWS and the advancement of earthquake science, it becomes increasingly clear that the effectiveness of these endeavors depends heavily on the precision and reliability of the detection methods employed. While significant progress has been made in this field, especially with the development of robust EEWS and the creation of comprehensive earthquake catalogs, challenges remain. The next section describes the limitations and challenges of traditional seismological signal detection methods, emphasizing the need for innovative solutions to enhance the accuracy and timeliness of earthquake detection.

1.2 Challenges in Traditional Seismological Signal Detection

Traditional seismological signal detection methods have been the cornerstone of earthquake monitoring for decades. These methods typically involve deploying a network of seismometers across a region to detect seismic waves generated by earthquakes. When an earthquake occurs, signals from multiple stations in the network are collected and analyzed to determine key characteristics of the event, such as its location, depth, and magnitude. This approach allows for the triangulation of the earthquake's epicenter and the estimation of its size, providing critical information that informs both scientific research and public safety measures.

However, while these traditional methods are robust and widely used, they also present several significant challenges. The effectiveness of these methods heavily relies on the density and distribution of the seismic network. In regions with sparse networks, it can be difficult to accurately pinpoint the location of an earthquake or assess its magnitude, leading to potential errors in the source characterization. Additionally, the process of collecting and analyzing data from multiple stations can introduce latency, which is particularly problematic in the context of earthquake early warning systems, where timely alerts are crucial. Furthermore, these methods can struggle to differentiate between various seismic sources, such as natural earthquakes, volcanic activity, or human-induced events, complicating the task of generating accurate earthquake catalogs.

One of the notable challenges in traditional seismological signal detection is the reliance on algorithms such as the Short-Term Average/Long-Term Average (STA/LTA) method (Allen, 1978), which is widely used to detect seismic events by identifying sudden increases in signal amplitude. Although effective in many cases, STA/LTA has some limitations, particularly in environments with low signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). In these situations, weak seismic signals can be obscured by background noise, leading to missed events (false negatives) or false alarms (false positives) (Vaezi and Van der Baan, 2015). Additionally, the method requires careful tuning of parameters, such as trigger thresholds and window lengths, which can be difficult to optimize in dynamic environments.

Microseismicity, which refers to very low-magnitude earthquakes, presents a significant challenge for traditional detection methods due to the low SNR. In areas with high levels of ambient noise, detecting these small events becomes even more difficult. Microseismic events are crucial as they can indicate stress changes within the Earth's crust and offer valuable insights into the processes leading up to larger seismic events. However, traditional algorithms often struggle with the detection and characterization of these weak signals, either missing them entirely or misclassifying them. Ross et al. (2016) introduced an advanced S-wave picking algorithm that leverages polarization filtering and more sophisticated detection techniques, improving the identification of weak seismic events even in noisy environments. This improvement underscores the limitations of traditional methods in regions with significant human activity, where background noise often obscures weaker seismic signals. Additionally, in areas with sparse seismic networks, the lack of data exacerbates the problem, leading to greater uncertainty in event location and magnitude estimates (Havskov and Alguacil, 2012).

Seismic swarms, characterized by numerous small to moderate earthquakes occurring over a short period, pose significant challenges for detection systems. Unlike mainshock-aftershock sequences, swarms lack a dominant large event, making it difficult for traditional methods like STA/LTA to detect individual events. The continuous seismic activity in swarms can overwhelm STA/LTA, causing it to miss important events, particularly when multiple earthquakes overlap. In the 2016 Bombay Beach swarm, Ross et al. (2018) observed overlapping earthquakes where the S-P times were as short as 1 second, adding complexity to event detection. STA/LTA struggles to reset quickly enough between events, often leading to missed or misclassified signals. Even human analysts are likely to miss many of these overlapping events due to the high frequency and complexity of the seismic activity. During the first 12 hours of the swarm, nearly 1,000 events were detected, approximately ten times more than what was manually cataloged.

Volcanic tremors, typically continuous, low-frequency signals generated by magma movement, pose a unique challenge for seismological detection systems. These signals can be difficult to distinguish from background noise or other non-seismic sources, especially because of their prolonged and persistent nature. As Chouet (1996) highlighted, volcanic tremors often feature long-period, harmonic waveforms that reflect pressure fluctuations and unsteady mass transport within the volcanic system. The interpretation of these tremors requires specialized techniques beyond conventional seismic detection, as their continuous and low-frequency characteristics are critical for understanding volcanic unrest and forecasting potential eruptions.

In the context of EEW, a significant challenge for traditional seismological detection methods is the occurrence of false alarms. Algorithms such as STA/LTA are highly sensitive to sudden increases in seismic activity, which can result in the detection of non-seismic signals or environmental noise. In areas with high background noise, such as urban settings or regions with substantial industrial activity, these algorithms may misinterpret non-seismic events as earthquakes, triggering false alarms. This can erode public confidence in EEWS, creating a "cry wolf" effect where individuals become desensitized to alerts, potentially ignoring real warnings when an actual earthquake occurs. Reducing false alarms is critical for maintaining the system's credibility and ensuring prompt public response during real seismic events.

False alarms also pose significant operational challenges for disaster response agencies, which may need to mobilize resources unnecessarily in response to these warnings. Heaton (1985) noted that the occurrence of false alarms can be particularly problematic in regions with sparse seismic networks or limited real-time data processing capacity. In such areas, the lack of sufficient data makes it difficult to confidently distinguish between true seismic events and false triggers, leading to a higher incidence of false alarms. This issue is exacerbated when ground motions are detected at great distances from the epicenter, increasing the uncertainty of the event's magnitude and location. As a result, response efforts can be misdirected or delayed, ultimately reducing the effectiveness of the overall earthquake early warning system.

The inability to provide accurate and timely early warnings is a critical limitation of traditional seismological detection methods, particularly in regions with limited resources. In many developing countries, the seismic infrastructure is often underfunded, resulting in sparse networks of seismometers that are unable to cover all seismically active areas effectively. Without a dense and comprehensive network, it becomes challenging to rapidly and accurately locate seismic events, especially smaller earthquakes. Allen and Melgar (2019) highlight that the effectiveness of earthquake early warning systems is highly dependent on the density of seismic networks and their ability to provide real-time data. In regions with inadequate infrastructure, delays in analyzing seismic data can lead to late warnings, reducing the overall effectiveness of the system in mitigating seismic hazards.

As these limitations become more apparent, the focus of seismological research is shifting toward more sophisticated technologies. The evolution of EEWS exemplifies this shift, where advancements in technology can significantly improve the accuracy and responsiveness of realtime earthquake detection. While current EEWS play a vital role in providing early warnings, their effectiveness is often constrained by the underlying detection algorithms. Addressing these constraints through technological innovations can dramatically enhance the performance of EEWS, particularly in terms of reducing false positives/negatives, improving detection of smaller seismic events, and providing more reliable early warnings.

Earthquake detection is increasingly being transformed by the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in geophysics, with Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) playing key roles. ML, a subset of AI, focuses on developing algorithms that can learn from data, identify patterns, and make decisions without explicit programming. These models are trained on historical data to predict or make decisions about new, unseen data. ML includes various approaches, such as supervised learning (learning from labeled data), unsupervised learning (finding patterns in unlabeled data), and reinforcement learning (learning through feedback or rewards). Deep Learning (DL), a further subset of ML, utilizes neural networks with multiple layers to mimic how the human brain processes information. DL is particularly effective in analyzing large and complex datasets, such as seismic waveforms, images, and audio. Its strength lies in detecting subtle patterns and performing tasks requiring high-level abstraction, making it invaluable for enhancing earthquake detection and other complex geophysical analyses.

AI offers robust tools for analyzing complex seismic data, identifying patterns and anomalies that may elude traditional methods. By integrating ML and DL into seismology, researchers are not only improving the detection capabilities of EEWS but also unlocking new insights into the mechanisms driving seismic activity. Exploring the potential of AI in seismic monitoring reveals how these technologies are transforming both EEWS and seismic hazard assessment, paving the way for a new era in earthquake detection.

In the following sections, we first conduct a thorough review of Earthquake Early Warning Systems, examining how these systems have evolved and the challenges they still face. We then delve into the foundations of AI, discussing its principles and the ways it is being applied in the field of seismology to address the limitations of traditional methods and to pave the way for a new era of seismic detection and analysis.

1.3 Present Earthquake Early Warning Systems

The development of EEWS marks a significant advancement in the field of seismology, providing critical alerts that can save lives and minimize damage during earthquakes. Through the years, the importance of an EEWS has grown even to the point that citizens themselves are willing to pay taxes to have it (Allen and Melgar, 2019). Gradually, EEWS have been adopted in various countries, starting with development and testing phases before expanding their capabilities to issue public alerts (Figure 1.4). The gradual evolution of these systems has enabled countries such as Japan, Mexico, the United States, etc., to integrate EEWS into their disaster management frameworks, allowing for early warnings that provide vital seconds for people to take protective actions before the strongest shaking arrives.

The practice of alerting the public to imminent earthquake shaking began in 1988 with the introduction of Japan's Urgent Earthquake Detection and Alarm System (UrEDAS). UrEDAS was the first operational system to analyze just a few seconds of P-waves recorded by a single station to rapidly estimate the earthquake's source parameters (Nakamura, 1988; Nakamura et al., 2011). This system represented a key milestone in earthquake early warning technology by providing fast estimates of the earthquake's magnitude and location, enhancing the ability to issue timely alerts.

It was not until 2007 that Japan, through the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), expanded its efforts to issue nationwide public earthquake warnings (Hoshiba, 2014). The system estimates the hypocenter and magnitude using P-wave data from stations near the epicenter, with magnitude estimates primarily based on peak displacement amplitudes. The system is capable of issuing public alerts via television, radio, mobile phones, and the internet, providing warnings to millions of people across Japan within seconds of an earthquake being detected (Hoshiba et al., 2008).

Mexico's EEWS or the 'Sistema de Alerta Sísmico Mexicano' (SASMEX), became the first system in the world to issue public alerts in 1993, predating Japan's public alerts (Suárez et al., 2018). SASMEX was initially designed to protect Mexico City from earthquakes originating along the Guerrero seismic gap, a region known for generating significant seismic activity (Espinosa Aranda et al., 1995). SASMEX operates by running three algorithms in parallel, each designed to enhance detection accuracy and ensure timely warnings. Alerts are triggered when at least two stations exceed a pre-established acceleration threshold, demonstrating a robust, multi-station approach to earthquake detection (Suárez, 2022). It currently broadcasts warnings to the populations of Acapulco, Chilpancingo, Morelia, Oaxaca, Puebla, Toluca, and Mexico City 2 .

SASMEX's detection algorithms are based on different aspects of the seismic signal, designed to alert earthquakes within the subducting Cocos plate. The first algorithm analyzes the first three seconds of the P-wave coda to estimate the event's magnitude (Cuéllar et al., 2018b). For more distant earthquakes within the Cocos plate, two additional algorithms were developed to enhance precision. The second algorithm evaluates the energy between the arrival times of the P-wave ( t p ) and the S-wave ( t s ) (Cuéllar et al., 2018a), while the third examines the energy within the period of 2( t p -t s ) to improve detection reliability (Cuéllar et al., 2017).

Taiwan has also been a pioneer in EEWS development, with the Central Weather Bureau (CWB) operating the system since 1995. Initially, it was designed for rapid seismic event reporting, supported by a real-time strong-motion network of 109 stations that could issue earthquake reports within 20 seconds of an event. In 2016, the CWB began providing public alerts through TV and mobile phones, with warnings issued within 15 seconds for regions with epicentral distances greater than 60 km (Wu et al., 2021).

To further enhance speed and accuracy, Taiwan integrated Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) accelerometers, which significantly lowered deployment costs and improved performance (Hsiao et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2013). This innovation led to the development of the 'Palert' device, a low-cost sensor that enabled the expansion of Taiwan's seismic network to 400 stations. The dense network provides accurate earthquake data and rapid tremor maps, ensuring timely warnings even in areas close to the epicenter (Wu et al., 2013), and issue on-site alarms when displacement thresholds are exceeded (Wu and Lin, 2014). Furthermore, the National Center for Research on Earthquake Engineering created an EEWS for schools, employing a MLalgorithm, specifically Support Vector Machine (SVM), that analyzes the first 3 seconds of vertical acceleration to predict Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) and issue on-site alarms (Hsu et al., 2021).

South Korea's EEWS (KEEWS) was launched in January 2015, operated by the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA). The system was initially designed to issue warnings within 50 seconds of detecting earthquakes with magnitudes of 5 or larger. The system is based on ElarmS-2 (Serdar Kuyuk et al., 2014), a well-established earthquake detection algorithm developed at the University of California, Berkeley, and was optimized for the seismic conditions of the Korean Peninsula by the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources (KIGAM). This optimization improved the system's ability to process local earthquake data and reduced false alerts caused by regional earthquakes.

To further improve performance, KEEWS incorporated the Triggered station spatial Distribution and azimuthal Bias (TrigDB) backfilling method, which helps prevent false event detections caused by regional or teleseismic earthquakes. In the system's first 18 months of operation, it successfully issued public alerts for several significant events, including a magnitude 5 offshore earthquake in July 2016 and a magnitude 5.8 earthquake on the southeastern Korean Peninsula in September 2016. KEEWS continues to evolve, with future plans to increase the number of seismic stations and improve response times for both inland and offshore events, ensuring greater accuracy and reliability in early warnings (Sheen et al., 2017).

The United States has also made significant strides in EEWS with the development of ShakeAlert, a system designed for the seismically active West Coast. ShakeAlert leverages a network of seismic sensors across California, Oregon, and Washington to detect earthquakes and issue warnings. Public alerts became available in California in 2019, and over the next few years, was gradually extended to include Oregon and Washington (Lux et al., 2024). The system uses real-time data processing to estimate the earthquake's magnitude, location, and expected intensity of shaking, providing alerts through various channels, including mobile notifications and automated responses for critical infrastructure (Burkett et al., 2014). Although ShakeAlert is still in its expansion phase, it represents a significant step forward in earthquake preparedness for the United States.

ShakeAlert was initially developed using three core algorithms, each designed to enhance earthquake detection and provide timely warnings. The first, the τ c -P d Onsite algorithm (Böse et al., 2009), uses the period parameter τ c and the peak initial-displacement amplitude P d (YihMin et al., 2007) - parameters widely used for EEWS purposes (Zollo et al., 2010) - from the first three seconds of the P-wave recorded by a single sensor. This algorithm combines the classic STA/LTA method (Allen, 1978) with a P/S wave discriminator that uses the ratio of horizontal to vertical ground motions. It estimates the earthquake's magnitude and Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) but does not determine its location, making it suitable for on-site warnings rather than regional alerts (Böse et al., 2014).

The second algorithm, the Virtual Seismologist (VS) (Cua, 2005), is a Bayesian approach designed for geographically distributed seismic hazards. VS estimates both the earthquake's magnitude and location by analyzing ground motion amplitudes and incorporating prior information such as network topology, fault locations, and station health. While it can estimate magnitude from the first three seconds of data from a single station, accurate location requires multiple stations (Cua et al., 2009).

The third algorithm, the Earthquake Alarm System (ElarmS), estimates earthquake magnitude by extracting peak displacement and maximum predominant frequency from broadband or strong-motion sensors (Brown et al., 2011). It also uses seismic wave arrival times to determine the earthquake's location and predicts ground shaking intensity using radial attenuation relationships (Allen, 2007).

Currently, ShakeAlert primarily relies on two key algorithms: the Earthquake Point-source Integrated Code (EPIC) and the Finite-fault Rupture Detector (FinDer). EPIC (Chung et al., 2019), an evolution of the original ShakeAlert algorithms, integrates the Onsite (Böse et al., 2009) and the third version of the Earthquake Alarm System (ElarmS-3) (Chung et al., 2019). It declares an event when at least four stations are triggered, each providing 0.2 seconds of seismic data. EPIC then estimates the earthquake's magnitude using four seconds of P-wave data from each station, based on Peak Displacement (Pd). FinDer (Böse et al., 2018a), on the other hand, estimates the earthquake's magnitude, rupture length, and orientation by comparing observed ground motions with predicted ground-motion templates.

Many countries are actively conducting real-time tests as they work toward launching public earthquake alert systems. In Chile, historically known for experiencing large earthquakes (Delouis et al., 2009, 2010), an EEWS for the northern region (Medina et al., 2022) utilizes the ElarmS-3 algorithm (Chung et al., 2019), successfully detecting and issuing alerts. Italy is also testing the PRESTo system (Satriano et al., 2011), which has been deployed in the southern part of the country, and is currently focused on real-time monitoring and EEW testing (Ladina et al., 2021). Notably, countries such as China (Peng et al., 2022), Israel (Nof et al., 2021), and others are in the advanced stages of real-time testing, and it is likely that more nations will implement EEWS in the near future as the need for earthquake preparedness grows globally.

The rapid evolution of EEWS globally has increasingly relied on advanced computational methods to boost speed and accuracy. A major advancement is the integration of AI into seismic signal processing, as exemplified Taiwan. AI techniques, including traditional machine learning and deep learning models, can swiftly analyze complex seismic waveforms, distinguish real events from noise, and estimate source characteristics with greater efficiency and precision than traditional methods. As these technologies evolve, they not only enhance existing systems but also open new possibilities for predictive modeling and faster, more reliable alerts. In the next section, we will explore how AI is revolutionizing seismology, focusing on machine learning methods for earthquake detection, magnitude estimation, and seismic hazard mitigation.

1.4 Artificial Intelligence in Seismology

AI is rapidly transforming numerous scientific disciplines, offering new ways to analyze large datasets, detect patterns, and make highly accurate predictions. In fields such as seismology (Mousavi and Beroza, 2023), healthcare (Giffard-Roisin et al., 2016, 2018), astrophysics (Fluke and Jacobs, 2020), and others, AI has enabled breakthroughs by automating complex tasks and revealing insights that were difficult to achieve with traditional methods. AI's strength lies in its ability to process real-time data with speed and precision, a capability now being harnessed in geophysics, particularly in seismology.

Before exploring AI applications in seismology, it is important to distinguish between two main AI techniques: traditional machine learning and its sub-discipline, deep learning. Traditional machine learning models, such as Support Vector Machines, Multilayer Perceptron, and Random Forests, rely on human-defined features and perform well on structured data. However, they require significant input to ensure relevant attributes are provided, offering the advantage of feature importance visualization. On the other hand, deep learning models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), automatically learn and extract features from raw data, making them particularly effective for unstructured data, such as images, audio, and time-series signals due to their self-optimization capability.

1.4.1 Overview of Traditional Machine Learning and Deep Learning

Traditional ML techniques rely on algorithms that use human-defined features, or attributes, to learn patterns from data. These models require careful feature selection and engineering, where domain knowledge plays a critical role in determining which attributes are most relevant for the task. They are highly effective for structured data, such as tabular datasets, where clear relationships between features and target variables can be defined. However, their performance is often limited by the quality of the features provided, necessitating significant human input during the data preprocessing and feature engineering phases.

The Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) is an extension of the simple perceptron, which was one of the earliest artificial neural network models. The perceptron consists of a single layer of neurons that processes inputs and produces an output, but it is limited in its ability to solve only linearly separable problems. To overcome this limitation, the MLP introduces multiple layers of neurons, creating a more complex architecture capable of handling non-linear relationships in the data (Popescu et al., 2009).

An MLP typically consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer (Figure 1.5). Each layer is fully connected, meaning every neuron in one layer is connected to every neuron in the next. The key innovation of the MLP is its use of the hidden layers and nonlinear activation functions, such as the sigmoid or Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU), which allow the network to learn more complex patterns in the data. During training, the MLP uses a process called backpropagation to adjust the weights of the connections between neurons, minimizing the error in predictions and enabling the model to generalize to unseen data.

The development of the MLP marked a significant advance over the original perceptron by enabling neural networks to solve a broader range of problems, particularly those involving complex, non-linear relationships. MLPs are foundational models in the field of neural networks, paving the way for the development of more advanced deep learning architectures.

Support Vector Machine (SVM) is another powerful traditional machine learning algorithm used for classification and regression tasks. The key idea behind SVM is to find the hyperplane that best separates data points belonging to different classes (for instance earthquakes and noises) in a high-dimensional space. The optimal hyperplane is the one that maximizes the margin, which is the distance between the hyperplane and the closest data points from each class

Figure 1.5 - MultiLayer Perceptron. Example of the architecture of a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with n human-defined input attributes, three hidden layers, and an output layer with n outputs (e.g., n = 2 for noise and earthquake classification). ( Taken from (Bre et al., 2018))

(Figure 1.6). These closest points, known as support vectors, play a crucial role in defining the boundary.

SVM can handle both linearly separable and non-linearly separable data. For non-linear cases, SVM uses a technique called the kernel trick, which transforms the input space into a higher-dimensional space where a linear separator can be found. Common kernels include the radial basis function (RBF), polynomial, and sigmoid. This ability to work in transformed spaces makes SVM a versatile and effective model, especially for tasks where clear decision boundaries are needed.

While SVM is highly effective for classification tasks, especially with smaller datasets, it requires careful tuning of hyperparameters such as the regularization parameter C (which controls the trade-off between maximizing the margin and minimizing classification error) and the choice of the kernel. Despite its strengths, SVM can struggle with large datasets, as its computational cost increases with the size of the data. Nonetheless, it remains a popular choice for a wide range of classification problems, such as Lara et al. (2020b).

Random Forest (RF) is also a traditional machine learning method that uses the ensembling method, which combines the predictions of multiple models, based on decision trees (Navada et al., 2011), to improve accuracy and robustness. RF constructs an ensemble of decision trees, where each tree is trained on a random subset of the training data and features. This method introduces variability among the trees, reducing the risk of overfitting and improving the model's generalization performance. By averaging or voting across all the trees in the forest, Random Forest provides a more stable and accurate prediction than any single tree.

The strength of Random Forest comes from its ability to mitigate the high variance typically seen in individual decision trees. While decision trees are simple and interpretable models, they tend to overfit, particularly when grown deep to capture complex relationships in the data. Random Forest combats this by averaging the results of many trees, thereby reducing overfitting and making the model more resilient to noise in the training data. Additionally, Random Forest provides useful insights into feature importance, helping to identify which attributes are most influential in making predictions.

Decision trees, the building blocks of Random Forests, have become increasingly important due to their role in modern boosting techniques, such as Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) (Chen and Guestrin, 2016a), Light Gradient-Boosting (LightGBM) (Ke et al., 2017), and Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost) (Freund and Schapire, 1997). These algorithms, while more sophisticated, still rely on decision trees as base learners. Boosting works by building trees sequentially, with each tree focusing on correcting the errors of the previous one. This iterative process leads to highly accurate models that excel in both classification and regression tasks. As a result, decision tree-based methods remain foundational in machine learning, powering many of the most effective algorithms in use today.

Boosting techniques, for instance XGB, have gained popularity due to their ability to apply parallelism for faster training. XGB leverages parallel processing to optimize the construction of decision trees, significantly speeding up the training process, especially for large datasets. It also supports Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) acceleration, further enhancing its perfor- mance by utilizing the power of modern hardware, making it much faster compared to algorithms such as SVM, which typically do not benefit from GPU acceleration. The combination of parallelism and GPU support makes XGB highly efficient and scalable for large-scale machine learning tasks.

The final prediction is obtained by aggregating the results of all decision trees through majority voting (for classification tasks) or averaging (for regression tasks). While boosting techniques such as XGB and LightGBM have pushed the limits of traditional machine learning by optimizing decision trees and exploiting modern hardware, they still rely on feature engineering and structured data. On the other hand, deep learning models, particularly neural networks such as CNN and RNN, excel in automatically learning features directly from raw, unstructured data. These models leverage large amounts of data and computational resources, particularly GPUs and Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), to discover patterns that traditional methods often miss, making them essential for tasks involving images, speech, and time-series data.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are a specialized type of deep learning model, primarily designed for handling grid-like data structures, such as images. What sets CNNs apart from traditional machine learning methods is their ability to automatically learn hierarchical features directly from raw data, without requiring extensive feature engineering. This makes CNNs highly effective for tasks such as image classification, object detection, and even video analysis. The key innovation behind CNNs is the convolution operation, which allows the model to scan input data (e.g., an image) using filters that detect various features, such as edges, textures, and patterns.

CNNs consist of multiple layers, including convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers (Figure 1.8). The convolutional layers apply filters to the input data to extract important features, while the pooling layers reduce the dimensionality, allowing the network to focus on the most significant information. The final fully connected layers aggregate this information to make predictions. The automatic feature extraction capability of CNNs makes them highly adaptable to complex and unstructured data, and their use of shared weights (filters) across the image makes them computationally efficient, especially when compared to fully connected neural networks.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a class of deep learning models specifically designed for handling sequential data, such as time-series, natural language, or audio signals. Unlike traditional neural networks, RNNs have a built-in memory mechanism that allows them to retain information from previous time steps, making them particularly effective for tasks where the order of the input matters. This is achieved through recurrent connections that loop back within the network, enabling it to pass information forward across time steps.

RNNs are widely used in tasks such as speech recognition, machine translation, and stock price prediction, where understanding the temporal dynamics of the data is crucial. However, standard RNNs face challenges when dealing with long-term dependencies, as they tend to forget information over longer sequences. To overcome this limitation, variations such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) were developed. These models incorporate gating mechanisms that allow them to retain or forget information as needed, making them more effective for handling longer sequences.

RNNs, and their variants like LSTMs and GRUs, are powerful tools in deep learning for sequence modeling, as they capture the temporal relationships and dependencies within data. They are particularly well-suited for real-time processing tasks and can handle both input sequences of varying lengths and complex dependencies over time. LSTMs introduce three key components: the forget gate ( f t ), which controls what information is discarded from the memory; input gate ( i t ), which regulates what new information is added to the memory; and output gate ( o t ), which determines what part of the memory is used to compute the current output (Figure 1.9). GRUs simplify this by merging the forget and input gates into a single update gate ( z t ), reducing the complexity while preserving the model's ability to retain long-term information.

Traditional machine learning algorithms and deep learning models have been, and continue to be, applied to various tasks in seismology, such as earthquake detection, aftershock forecasting, etc. Traditional ML models are especially valuable for their ability to provide insights into the importance of individual features (attributes), offering interpretable results that can help researchers gain a deeper understanding of the underlying seismic processes. In contrast, deep learning models, while less interpretable, excel at automatically extracting patterns from raw data, which can be particularly useful when handling large and complex datasets. The choice between traditional machine learning and deep learning depends on the specific problem at hand, with each approach offering distinct advantages.

The following section describes how AI, through both traditional machine learning and deep learning approaches, is applied to address key challenges in seismology. These methods improve the processing of seismic data, enhance earthquake early warning systems, and support aftershock prediction, among other applications, contributing to more informed decisionmaking in earthquake preparedness and mitigation efforts.

1.4.2 Application of AI in Seismology

Seismology, traditionally reliant on a combination of deterministic and probabilistic models grounded in physical principles, is increasingly adopting machine learning techniques to enhance earthquake detection, magnitude estimation, seismic risk assessments, and other tasks within the field. Machine learning has proven invaluable for automating processes that previously required extensive manual effort. where machine learning has become a primary focus (Figure 1.10) of scientific research and application (Mousavi and Beroza, 2023). ML algorithms significantly reduces the workload of seismologists by efficiently distinguishing between different types of seismic signals. For instance, after a large mainshock, numerous aftershocks occur, and ML models streamline the classification process, enhancing the precision of seismic catalogs.

Seismic networks generate vast amounts of data that need to be processed and analyzed in real time. Traditional seismic detection methods rely on manual or semi-automated waveform analysis, which can be time-consuming and prone to human error. AI models, such as CNNs and RNNs, can automate the process of seismic data analysis, learning from large datasets and processing information in a fraction of the time required by traditional methods. For instance, CNNs have been used to analyze continuous seismic records to detect microseismicity that may have been overlooked using conventional methods (Anikiev et al., 2023). Moreover, AI models are scalable, allowing them to process data from thousands of seismic stations simultaneously, making them invaluable for large, seismically active regions such as Japan, California, and Taiwan.

Machine learning has also been transformative in volcanic event classification, where vari- ous seismo-volcanic phenomena-such as long-period events, tremors, explosions, and hybrid events-can manifest in large quantities daily (Lara et al., 2020b). The ability of ML to automatically and accurately classify these events eases the burden on seismologists in seismic observatories. Beyond these applications, ML has also been instrumental in distinguishing between local and teleseismic events (Mousavi et al., 2019b), classifying seismic events by source depth (Mousavi et al., 2016), discriminating earthquakes from quarry blasts (Saad et al., 2022b), and other types of seismic classifications. The widespread adoption of ML in these tasks highlights its crucial role in simplifying the daily operations of seismic research and monitoring centers.

Mousavi and Beroza (2022) present a comprehensive overview of how deep learning has been integrated into seismology, highlighting its transformative impact on multiple tasks. Deep learning techniques such as CNNs and RNNs have demonstrated the ability to significantly outperform traditional methods in areas such as earthquake detection, creating refined catalogs with a higher number of detections, phase selection improving the accuracy of arrival times, and seismic image processing. These advances are largely attributed to deep learning's ability to handle noisy, high-dimensional data and automatically extract meaningful features without requiring manual intervention.

The increase in the application of DL models to seismology began to grow exponentially from ∼ 2016 onward (Figure 1.11). The number of papers published annually on the topic surged, with over 600 papers published by 2020 (Mousavi and Beroza, 2022). This growth is accompanied by a significant rise in the complexity of the neural network models used, as indicated by the increasing average number of neural network hidden layers. The figure also shows a clear trend of larger training datasets, with many studies now utilizing datasets exceeding 400,000 samples. The exponential growth of the number of published articles highlights the rapid adoption of deep learning techniques in seismology, driven by advancements in computational power and the availability of large seismic datasets.

One of the most prominent applications of deep learning in seismology is the generation of earthquake catalogs. Traditional methods often struggle to detect smaller events, resulting in incomplete catalogs. However, deep learning models have enabled the creation of far more detailed catalogs, identifying events that would otherwise go unnoticed. For instance, the PhaseNet algorithm (Zhu and Beroza, 2019), trained using deep learning, significantly outperforms the traditional AR picker (Akazawa, 2004) in estimating P and S phase arrivals. PhaseNet achieves a mean error and standard deviation of 2.0 ms and 51.53 ms for P-phase arrival, com- pared to 11.65 ms and 83.99 ms for the AR picker. The advantage is even more pronounced in S-phase arrivals, where PhaseNet's performance surpasses traditional methods like STA/LTA, particularly because the S wave is often obscured by the P-wave coda. Similarly, the deep learning-based EQTransformer outperforms STA/LTA in event detection, achieving a perfect precision and recall of 1.0, compared to STA/LTA's 0.91 and 1.0. Moreover, EQTransformer excels in automatic phase picking, with a MAE of 0.01 s, surpassing traditional methods such as Kurtosis (Saragiotis et al., 2002), FilterPicker (Lomax et al., 2012), and AIC (Maeda, 1985) by more than 0.07 s for P-phase estimates and over 0.09 s for S-phase estimates.

Several machine learning algorithms have been developed for tasks in seismology (Mousavi and Beroza, 2023, 2022; Al Banna et al., 2020), including magnitude estimation, location estimation, PGA prediction, among others. While deep learning excels in data-rich tasks, it also faces challenges with sparse data, particularly for rare, large-magnitude earthquakes.

For instance, if a MEMS-based EEWS is needed (because the low cost), traditional machine learning models are often more suitable due to their lower computational requirements, faster processing speeds, and ability to operate efficiently on resource-constrained devices. Algorithms such as Support Vector Machines or Decision Tree-based ensemble models (e.g. XGB) can be easily installed on devices such as Raspberry Pi (a low-cost, credit card-sized computer), allowing for rapid classification of seismic events and onsite estimation of the source characterization, which is crucial for EEWS. In contrast, deep learning models, while often more accurate and capable of automatic feature extraction, typically demand more computational power and are slower, making them less practical for MEMS without additional edge computing resources. Thus, unless integrated with external computing support, traditional ML models provide a more reliable solution for real-time earthquake detection and alerting on MEMS devices. A clear example is the Taiwanese EEWS (Hsiao et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2013), which incorporates MEMS stations, or the Raspberry Shakes (seismic sensors based on Raspberry Pi) network in Haiti, deployed in urban homes to enhance understanding of seismic activity in the region (Calais et al., 2022).

Mousavi and Beroza (2022) highlight the need for hybrid approaches that combine deep learning with physics-based models to ensure reliability in such cases. An example is PEGSNet (Licciardi et al., 2022a), an algorithm that estimates the instantaneous magnitude of an earthquake from elasto-gravity signals. PEGSNet was trained using a CNN with a synthetic database generated from physical equations (Juhel et al., 2019).

Future efforts should focus on developing explainable AI models to bridge the gap between neural network outputs and the underlying seismic processes. However, despite significant progress in ML applications for seismic tasks, fewer models have been specifically designed for EEWS. According to the article database related to AI in seismology 3 , only 15 out of 809 articles were specifically related to EEW purposes as of 2022, and only 2 of them are based on single station. In recent years, additional works have emerged addressing components of EEWS, such as detection and source characterization estimation. However, to date, no fully AI-based EEWS has been designed, which is the main focus of this thesis and will be discussed in the following section. Furthermore, as shown in Figure 1.10, the use of ensemble methods has not been widely explored.

Single-station EEWS is particularly important in subduction zones near populated areas, where the proximity of seismic activity leaves little time for regional warnings. Autonomous systems powered by machine learning could issue alerts within seconds, offering crucial protection in these high-risk regions. This thesis aims to revive single-station EEWS by proposing a machine learning-based system that improves temporal response, independently detects earthquakes and estimates source characterization (usable in other contexts), while also providing deeper insights into seismic processes, addressing key gaps in AI-based early warning systems.

Earthquake Early Warning Starting From 3 s of Records on a Single Station With Machine Learning

Chapter 2 introduces the Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System (E3WS), that uses Ensemble machine learning to detect, locate, and estimate earthquake magnitudes starting from 3 seconds of P-wave records from a single station. This system, the first EEWS entirely designed with AI algorithms, provides significant improvements in speed and accuracy compared to existing single-station methods. E3WS has been tested with data from Peru, Chile, Japan, and the STEAD global dataset, and is already operational in alpha mode as the core of the Peruvian EEWS. This chapter was written in collaboration with Quentin Bletery , Jean-Paul Ampuero , Adolfo Inza , and Hernando Tavera , and published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth under the title 'Earthquake Early Warning Starting From 3 s of Records on a Single Station With Machine Learning' (Lara et al., 2023).
