3.4.4 SASPe performance in real time

Recently, in June 2024, the department of Arequipa experienced significant seismic activity, including a M 7 earthquake on June 28, 2024, along with a M 6.3 foreshock on June 16 and a M 6.4 aftershock on June 29. We present the performance of SASPe during the M 7 earthquake of June 28, 2024 (Fig. 3.10). Although public alarms are not yet available, the IGP issues internal alert messages as part of its testing protocol. This involves storing the estimated magnitude and hypocenter, and calculating the alert radius. Additionally, an audible alarm is activated at the Centro Sismológico Nacional (CENSIS) located at the IGP facilities in Lima, and the simulated alert message is simultaneously sent to the COER and stored on the IGP servers. This event is a compelling example to illustrate the functionality of SASPe because of its proximity to a large city such as Arequipa, which has previously experienced significant earthquakes such as the 2001 Mw 8.4 and 2018 Mw 7.2 events. Moreover, we present the performance of SASPe for the June foreshock and aftershock, along with two other recorded M ≥ 6 earthquakes from our database described in Section 3.3, in the supplementary information (Fig. S5 - S8).

Purple dotted line represents the 5% g acceleration threshold in the SASPe alert radius. (b) Tolerances in the alert radius as a function of time relative to the P-wave arrival time at the nearest station for M ≥ 6 earthquakes.

The earthquake occurred on the Peruvian subduction fault at a depth of 42 km, as reported by IGP. E3WS detected the earthquake using seismic records from the second nearest station, with the initial magnitude estimate (based on 3 seconds of P wave) being M = 6, slightly larger than the first estimate of M = 5.9 from the closest station, with only a 0.4-second difference in detection times. SASPe estimated the P wave arrival time at 9.5 seconds after the earthquake origin time. This information was sent to the COER and IGP.

We define the user lead time (theoretical) as the difference between the arrival time of the S-wave at a specific geographic location and the arrival of the first simulated alert message at the COERs and IGP. We ignore transmission delays but take into account processing delays, including the time taken to generate the feature vector, the time needed to estimate the source characterization, and an additional 3 seconds for the initial estimate (first estimate based on 3 s of P wave). Lead times ranged from 7.7 seconds for areas closest to the epicenter to over 30 seconds at the SASPe-issued alert radius limits. For areas with the highest PGA ( > 45%g), lead times ranged from 7.7 to 10 seconds, while users slightly further away with PGA > 30%g had lead times of up to 20 seconds.

We assessed the accuracy of the SASPe alarm by comparing it with the actual area where PGA > 5% (based from USGS, https://earthquake.usgs.gov/ ). The area where an alert was correctly issued and the earthquake impact was significant (PGA > 5%g) was classified as a true positive (TP). A false positive (FP) was defined as the area where an alert was issued, but the earthquake impact was not significant. Lastly, a false negative (FN) referred to the area where no alert was issued, but the earthquake impact was significant. We calculated precision and recall as: precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN).

SASPe estimated an alert area of approximately 39,000 km 2 , while the actual region that experienced a PGA > 5% was 40,000 km 2 . SASPe achieved both a precision and recall of 90% for this earthquake. The high precision indicates that only 10% of the areas that should not have been alerted (white region inside the purple circle in Fig. 3.10) were mistakenly alerted. The high recall signifies that only 10% of the areas that should have been alerted were missed. These areas experienced a maximum PGA of 7.8%g, which is below the 10%g threshold considered dangerous for precarious housing. The use of tolerances allowed SASPe to cover nearly the entire risk zone, as compared to the area covered by the theoretical alert radius (blue circle), reflecting a conservative approach aimed at covering all areas experiencing significant accelerations.

3.4.5 E3WS around the world

We assess the performance of the E3WS algorithm for major earthquakes that occurred in 2023 and 2024 worldwide (Table 3.2) to showcase the portability of the algorithm. We simulate the real-time processing and adhere to the same criteria for disseminating the alert message as prescribed by SASPe (M ≥ 6 trigger threshold to issue alarms). In all instances, the actual magnitude (from USGS) exceeds 6, and the E3WS magnitude estimate based on the first 3 s of data from the station nearest to the source also indicates M ≥ 6. Furthermore, these estimates persist as M ≥ 6 for longer windows. In some cases, it is possible to estimate the final earthquake magnitude using 9 seconds of the P wave at the closest station, as observed in the 2023 M 6.8 Marrakech earthquake in Morocco. Notably, E3WS demonstrates its capability to provide accurate estimates even with saturated seismograms, such as those observed at SDPT and TIO stations, which are broadband sensor stations nearest to the 2023 Alaska and Morocco earthquakes, respectively.

We compute the user lead time provided by E3WS as the difference between the arrival time of the S wave and the time E3WS identifies that the magnitude exceeds 6. In all cases, the user lead time around the location with the greatest loss of life (excluding Alaska, where there were no fatalities) is positive. Time provided to the user ranges from 0.2 seconds for the 2023 Marrakech earthquake to 13.7 seconds for the Alaska earthquake in 2023, and extends to 30 seconds for the 2024 Noto earthquake in cities that reported human losses. The lead time in Marrakech is short (0.2 s) because this city is closer to the epicenter than the nearest station to the epicenter (TIO), highlighting the importance of having a station as close to the source as possible in an EEWS. For users near the TIO station, E3WS provides 10 s of lead time.

In the case of the January 1st 2024 Noto earthquake, we computed the user lead times as the difference between the time when E3WS identified an M ≥ 6 earthquake and the time at which ground acceleration reached 5% g , to provide a more practical metric, leveraging the high density of ground motion recordings in Japan. The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) cataloged two sub-events during this earthquake: a M 5.9 at 07:10:09.5 UTC and a M 7.6 at 07:10:22.6. As both sub-events were very close in time, only 12 s apart, E3WS detected and estimated the magnitude of the first sub-event as M ≥ 6 at 3.4 s after the earthquake origin time. This rapid response is a result of the very short distance between the station and the seismic source. For users in the city of Suzu, which experienced the highest number of human losses (103), the alert would arrive 2.2 s before the earthquake shaking exceeded 5% g . For neighboring cities such as Wajima, where there was a significant number of human losses (102), the E3WS algorithm would have generated 11 s of lead time. Furthermore, for more remote cities with fatalities such as Anamizu, Nanao, Shika and Hakui, E3WS would have provided 13.4, 19.3, 30, and 15 seconds of lead time, respectively.

3.5 Discussion

3.5.1 Accuracy of alerts

The performance of SASPe during the M 7 earthquake in Arequipa, as shown in Figure 3.10, demonstrates that even with an initial underestimation (based on 3 seconds of P-wave from a single station), the system's tolerances, based on E3WS uncertainties, effectively compensated for the theoretical alert radius. This allowed the system to cover nearly the entire area where PGA > 5%g, resulting in high precision and recall of 90%. This accuracy underscores SASPe's effectiveness in providing timely and accurate alerts. However, in other recorded earthquakes with magnitudes between 6.1 and 6.8 (Fig. S5-S8), the average precision dropped to 23%, while recall remained consistently at 100%. This suggests that although all areas that should have been alerted were covered, a significant portion of the alerts were issued for regions that did not experience damaging ground motions.

For the vast majority of M ≥ 6 earthquakes, E3WS accurately estimates magnitudes larger than 6 in its initial estimate, as shown in Figs. 3.7 and 3.10 and Lara et al. (2023). This accuracy is further demonstrated in the earthquakes shown in Figs. S5-S8, where the M6.1, M6.3, M6.4, and M6.8 events were initially estimated by SASPe as M6.4, M6, M6, and M6.3, respectively. This is particularly relevant in Peru, where the average annual number of earthquakes with magnitudes larger than 6 is 3, with a STD of 2. However, on rare occasions, E3WS may overestimate an earthquake with a magnitude smaller than 6 as being larger than 6 Lara et al. (2023). Given the SASPe network of independently operated stations, such occurrences could be possible. Therefore, to provide useful alert messages, the system must often over-alert (issue alerts for lower magnitudes and/or expand the alert radius), meaning users need to be tolerant of false alerts Minson et al. (2019). This tolerance is not about earthquakes not occurring but rather about experiencing ground motion less than PGA 5%g due to these events. While increasing the alert threshold might reduce the number of false positives, it would also increase the number of missed alerts, which are generally more costly than false alerts Minson et al. (2022).

To address this, SASPe's Component 4, led by INDECI (Peru's emergency management agency), will play a crucial role in training the population to interact with the system effectively. Through preparedness activities, such as drills and evacuation plans, INDECI will help Peruvians become accustomed to responding to alerts, even when the ground motion is less intense than expected. This proactive engagement will strengthen the population's ability to handle future seismic events while maintaining trust in SASPe.

3.5.2 Lead times for nearby megathrust earthquakes

Weevaluate user lead times based on the SASPe network for earthquakes along the Peruvian subduction megathrust using simulated earthquake scenarios. We consider hypothetical sources on a 0 . 05 ◦ -spacing grid (in both latitude and longitude), with depths shallower than 60 km, along the Peruvian subduction megathrust using the slab geometry given by the Slab2 model Hayes et al. (2018). We consider another 0 . 05 ◦ -spacing grid along the coastal region of Peru (receiver grid) to calculate theoretical lead times for earthquakes within 100 km of epicentral distance from each receiver location. We compute the user lead time by subtracting 3 s (E3WS first estimate delay) from the difference between the S-wave arrival time at the analyzed location and the P-wave arrival time at the nearest SASPe station. We ignore transmission delays but take into account processing delays as in Section 3.4.4. For each point on the receiver grid, we calculate the average user lead times (Fig. 3.11a) and their STD (Fig. 3.11b).

Our analysis reveals that SASPe typically provides user lead times ranging from 9 to 11 seconds for residents near the Peruvian coast, where the epicentral distance is between 62 km and 73 km. In Tumbes and specific areas of Piura, however, the lead times slightly decrease, ranging from 7 to 9 seconds for epicentral distances between 54 km and 64 km. For communities further inland, where epicentral distances span from 73 km to 83 km, lead times consistently remain between 11 and 13 seconds. In more isolated regions, where distances exceed 94 km, lead times extend beyond 15 seconds.

The STD of lead times ranges from 2 to 4 seconds near the coast in central Peru and the departments of Ica and northern Arequipa. In northern Peru, STDs vary from 4 to 7 seconds, while in southern Arequipa and the southernmost departments, they range from 4 to 6 seconds. For the more remote areas with epicentral distances exceeding 85 km, the STDs range between 0 and 2 seconds.

Furthermore, we calculated user lead times for two historical earthquakes that occurred approximately 60 km offshore of Lima on October 3, 1974 (M 7.7), and November 9, 1974 (M 7.2). Using theoretical travel times, we estimate that SASPe would have provided mean ± STD lead times of 12.6 ± 3.2 seconds for the M7.7 earthquake and 12.1 ± 2.2 seconds for the M7.2 earthquake for locations 100 km away from the epicenter. These results are consistent with those depicted in Fig. 3.11 and validate the effectiveness of SASPe in providing, typically, timely alerts.

3.5.3 Late-alert zone

We assess the existence of late alert zones in Peru, where SASPe may fail to provide a minimum 3-second lead time for performing drop, cover, and hold on. We indicate the locations where the S-wave has already arrived within 3 seconds by the time SASPe broadcasts the alert message. Considering SASPe's purpose to monitor potentially hazardous earthquakes on the subduction fault, we consider the same grid of sources and receivers, and the same processing and transmission delays as in Section 3.5.2. For each location on the grid of receivers, we select the earthquake from the grid of sources whose S-wave has the shortest source-site travel time.

The analysis reveals that all 10 departments along the Peruvian coast can exhibit positive user lead times, typically ranging from 0 to 10 or 20 seconds for the most critical cases (Fig. 3.12). In the departments of Piura, Lambayeque and Ica, earthquakes originating in specific locations can result in negative lead times at some locations, while in Tumbes, Lima, and Arequipa, lead times are positive but less than 3 seconds in some locations. However, the alert remains useful away from these specific locations. Note that the map shows the worst-case scenario for each location.

We also computed the lead times for very large earthquakes (M ≥ 7 shallower than 100 km) that occurred in Peru since 1970. In 88% of the cases, we observe positive lead times, primarily falling between 0 and 15 seconds. Some events have minimum alert times between 0 and 5 seconds, for instance the M 8 2007 Pisco earthquake (department of Ica) with a lead time of 4.2 seconds. The only two events for which we obtain negative minimum lead times are two non-subduction earthquakes: the Mw 7.1 earthquake that occurred in the Peruvian rain forest in 1991 at 20 km depth Alva-Hurtado et al. (1992) and the Mw 7.1 Macas earthquake in Ecuador in 1995, at a depth of 24 km Alvarado et al. (1996). For these two events, the lead time at the nearest district would be negative. However, these types of earthquakes exceed magnitude 6 more rarely than subduction earthquakes, which are the focus of SASPe. Since 1970, 14% of all earthquakes shallower than 100 km with magnitudes larger than 6 were caused by offsubduction faults, and only 12% (2 earthquakes) with M ≥ 7. Unfortunately, it is likely that E3WS misses these earthquakes (the detector would not trigger) since they are more than 200 km away from the epicenter, beyond its maximum training distance.

3.6 Conclusion

Wepresent the performance of the seismological components of SASPe, the newly-implemented Peruvian earthquake early warning system. The system uses the E3WS algorithm and determines its first alert using the initial 3 s of P-wave data recorded by the nearest station to the seismic source. During a testing period extending over more than 2 years, SASPe successfully detected 1,973 earthquakes with magnitudes exceeding 3. For all M ≥ 6 earthquakes, the estimated magnitudes are consistently larger than 6, while all estimates for earthquakes below magnitude 6 are below 6. Consequently, given the trigger threshold of M ≥ 6 for broadcasting alert messages, SASPe had no false positives or false negatives. SASPe enhances the location estimation of the E3WS algorithm, initially based on a single station, by incorporating data from all stations with P-wave recordings available when the closest station captures 3 seconds of earthquake records. Additionally, SASPe provides tolerances that must be added to the estimated alert radius to compensate for errors in seismic source characterization estimates, ensuring that citizens who should receive the alert message do not miss it. Continuous updates of magnitude and location estimates enable fine-tuning of the optimal alert radius. SASPe can typically generate user lead times ranging from 9 to 11 seconds for areas closest to the Peruvian coast and over 15 seconds for regions where epicentral distances exceed 94 km. In the worst-case scenarios, SASPe can provide up to 8 seconds of lead time for populations nearest to the seismic source and 10 to 20 seconds or more for regions farther away (70 to 120 km of distance). The first devices for broadcasting alert messages to the public have already been constructed in six districts of Lima, with plans for completion along the entire Peruvian coast by the year 2025.

E3WS for seismic monitoring in different sparsely-instrumented contexts

Although E3WS was designed for early warning applications, it can be configured for other purposes, such as detecting earthquakes and estimating magnitude and location using data from a single station. Chapter 4 presents applications of E3WS to different research projects unrelated to early warning. We use E3WS to build seismic catalogs in sparsely-instrumented areas. In Haiti, we show that foreshock forecasting is as accurate using the seismic catalog obtained by applying E3WS to a single low-cost seismic station as using the seismic catalog obtained from the entire regional seismic network with conventional approaches. In Colombia, we explore the use of E3WS to monitor seismic swarm activity. In Ecuador, we find that E3WS detects short-term seismic swarms some associated to potential slow slip events and others triggered by teleseismic surface waves - that were undetected by previous studies relying on multiple stations. Finally, we analyze the foreshock sequence leading up to the 2024 Arequipa earthquake.

4.1 Aftershock Forecasting in Haiti

This work was part of a collaboration with a large group of people: Éric Calais, Steeve Symithe, Tony Monfret, Bertrand Delouis, Anthony Lomax, Françoise Courboulex, JeanPaul Ampuero, Quentin Bletery, Jérôme Chèze, Fabrice Peix, Anne Deschamps, Bernard De Lépinay, Bryan Raimbault, Romain Jolivet, Sylvert Paul, Sadrac St Fleur, Dominique Bozisson, Yo Fukushima, Zacharie Duputel, Liuwei Xu and Lingsen Meng . It was published in Science under the title Citizen seismology helps decipher the 2021 Haiti earthquake (Calais et al., 2022).

On 14 August 2021, a Mw 7.2 earthquake struck the Nippes region of southern Haiti, resulting in approximately 2,500 deaths, 13,000 injuries, and the destruction or damage of over 140,000 homes. The epicenter was located near the Enriquillo-Plantain Garden Fault Zone, a major tectonic boundary in the region (Fig. 4.1), and it was one of the most powerful earthquakes Haiti had experienced since the devastating Mw 7.0 earthquake in 2010. The earthquake primarily affected rural areas with low population density, although severe damage occurred in the more populated cities of Les Cayes and Jérémie. The aftermath was further complicated by a tropical storm that followed the earthquake, as well as ongoing issues of insecurity and limited access to affected regions.

The seismic network in Haiti, particularly during the 2021 Nippes earthquake, was largely supported by the citizen-based Raspberry Shake (RS) seismic stations. This network, known as the Ayiti-seismes "seismo-citizen" platform, was established in 2019 and is composed of lowcost seismometers installed in homes, schools, and public buildings, providing crucial real-time seismic data in regions with limited formal infrastructure. These stations, composed by singlecomponent vertical velocimeters and three-component accelerometers, are hosted by private individuals who provide internet access, electricity and safety. Although ambient noise can sometimes affect data quality, there are currently 15 operational stations across Haiti, offering essential seismic information.

The platform uses an automated earthquake detection system based on Seiscomp3 modules, combined with software developed at Géoazur, and processes data from RS seismometers in Haiti along with regional stations in neighboring countries such as Cuba and the Dominican Republic. The system outputs real-time earthquake locations and magnitudes through a web interface ( https://ayiti.unice.fr/ayiti-seismes ), and the data is regularly reviewed by seismologists to maintain an updated earthquake catalog, which is publicly available. Data and metadata are also accessible through Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks (FDSN) protocols.

The Ayiti-seismes platform has provided rapid seismic information for events of magnitude larger than 2.5, and, under certain conditions, has detected events as small as magnitude 1.4-2.0. During the August 14, 2021 Mw 7.2 Nippes earthquake, three RS instruments were installed near the epicenter, with one fully operational at the time of the earthquake. The other two stations, temporarily offline due to internet issues, were restored shortly after the event. The system's flexibility enabled the deployment of two additional stations in the epicentral area within a few days after the earthquake, demonstrating the potential of community-driven seismic monitoring in regions with limited infrastructure.

The R50D4 station, part of the Haiti citizen network, played a crucial role in recording the seismic activity during the seismic event. Located only 21 kilometers away from the epicenter (Fig. 4.1), the station captured critical real-time data using its accelerometric sensors. Despite being hosted in a residential setting, the station recorded the mainshock without saturation, with peak ground acceleration reaching 0.33 g on its north-south component. This level of acceleration, particularly for periods under 0.5 seconds, helps explain the extensive damage observed in the region, where most structures were not built to earthquake-resistant standards.

To forecast the evolution of aftershocks, we applied the method developed by Reasenberg and Jones (1989, 1994), which utilizes two well-established empirical relations in statistical seismology: the Gutenberg-Richter law of magnitude distribution and the Omori-Utsu law of aftershock rate decay. This method does not account for secondary aftershocks (aftershocks of aftershocks), focusing only on the primary aftershock sequence.

Using maximum-likelihood estimates, we determined the productivity ( K ) and time scale ( c ) of the aftershock sequence. The daily rates of aftershocks were evaluated using a nonstationary Poisson process, and we computed 90% confidence intervals for the expected aftershock activity, providing a probabilistic framework for forecasting the aftershock decay.

We applied this forecasting technique to two independent datasets. First, we utilized an aftershock catalog derived from the Ayiti-seismes network. Second, we applied it to an aftershock catalog generated from data recorded by a single RS station (R50D4) located near the earthquake rupture. To build this second catalog, we used the E3WS algorithm to detect earthquakes with magnitudes larger than 3. We trained the E3WS detector using the compiled earthquake database (see Chapter 2) with noise data recorded by station R50D4. We then applied it to the vertical geophone data from station R50D4. Although E3WS typically requires data from three channels to perform its estimations, we adapted it in this case to work with a single channel by replicating the vertical channel as a substitute for the horizontal channels.

The aftershock catalog generated by E3WS using only the R50D4 data was in strong agreement with the catalog created by the full seismic network in Haiti. Notably, in the early stages of aftershock detection, the single-station system outperformed the broader network by detecting more earthquakes (Fig. 4.2), demonstrating the ability of a single, well-located station to function effectively even in resource-limited environments.

By fitting the obtained aftershock distributions for the first 12 hours to the Omori-Utsu law, we found that the catalog derived from E3WS provided accurate forecasts for aftershock decay rates, with 95% confidence intervals (Fig. 4.2). As the fitting time window increased, E3WS predictions showed even better alignment with observed aftershock activity compared to traditional catalog-based forecasts, particularly at fitting times of 48 and 96 hours. This success underscores the potential of low-cost, citizen-operated seismic stations combined with ML algorithms for reliable real-time aftershock detection and forecasting. The application of E3WS in Haiti highlights the scalability of the algorithm and its suitability for regions where infrastructure is limited, providing a tool for earthquake early warning and aftershock forecast.

4.2 Characterizing swarm seismicity in Colombia

This work is part of the Bachelor's thesis of Juan Andrés Montenegro , a student from Universidad de los Andes, whom I co-advised. His thesis focused on seismic monitoring in Colombia (Montenegro Folleco, 2023).

Colombia's complex tectonic environment, characterized by the interaction of multiple tectonic plates and frequent seismic activity, presents challenges and opportunities for seismic monitoring. In particular, the Murindó and Cauca regions are prone to seismic swarms, making them interesting locations to apply advanced detection methods to better understand these phenomena.

Although E3WS was designed for early warning applications, it can be reconfigured for other purposes, such as detecting earthquakes and estimating magnitude and location using data from a single station. In this chapter, we apply E3WS to the Murindó and Cauca regions to enhance our understanding of seismic swarm behavior and to explore the potential of singlestation monitoring in complex tectonic settings.

Colombia is located in a highly tectonically active region due to the interaction of several major tectonic plates: the Nazca, South American, and Caribbean plates, along with the Panama-Chocó block (Fig. 4.3). These interactions result in significant seismic activity, making Colombia one of the most seismically active countries in South America. The complex tectonic setting generates a wide range of seismic events, from large megathrust earthquakes along subduction zones to shallow crustal seismicity inland. Understanding this seismicity is crucial for assessing seismic hazards and risks in the region.

The Murindó and Cauca regions have experienced frequent seismic swarms, characterized by a series of earthquakes clustered in time and space without a clear mainshock. Historical records from the Servicio Geológico Colombiano (SGC) provide context for understanding the seismic characteristics of these regions. In the Murindó cluster, over 6,300 seismic events have been recorded between 1993 and 2023, with magnitudes typically ranging from 1 to 4.7. Similarly, the Cauca region has experienced around 8,000 recorded events over the same period, with magnitudes up to 6.6.

These swarms pose challenges for seismic monitoring due to:

- High Event Frequency: The rapid succession of events can make it difficult to distinguish individual earthquakes.
- Low-Magnitude Events: Small events may go undetected by distant stations, leading to incomplete catalogs.

- Sparse Network Coverage: Limited seismic stations in remote areas reduce detection accuracy.

The primary objectives of applying E3WS to the Murindó and Cauca regions are to evaluate its detection capabilities within earthquake swarms, characterize swarm behavior, and demonstrate E3WS's versatility beyond early warning applications. In this study, E3WS was configured to run on a 10-minute window surrounding each of the 68 earthquakes in Murindó and 42 in Cauca, recorded from 2016 to 2023, within 200 km of the HEL and PAL stations, respectively. This targeted application verifies E3WS's ability to detect all cataloged events, including smaller magnitudes within swarm sequences, without running the algorithm continuously over the entire study period.

We applied E3WS to the seismic stations Santa Helena (HEL) near the Murindó cluster and San Jose del Palmar (PAL) near the Cauca cluster. The methodology involved collecting historical seismic data from these stations, processing them, and estimating earthquake magnitudes and locations with E3WS.

E3WS successfully detected all 68 known seismic events recorded in the region during the study period (Fig. 4.4). The magnitude estimation achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.24 compared to the SGC catalog, highlighting the system's accuracy in magnitude assessment. The MAE for epicentral distance was 13.6 km, reflecting reliable distance estimation. For the Cauca cluster, E3WS successfully identified all 42 known earthquakes recorded in the region, despite the low SNR conditions often encountered at the PAL station, where signal quality frequently drops below 10 dB. This low SNR posed challenges for accurately estimating certain parameters; nonetheless, the system achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.33 in magnitude estimation, demonstrating solid performance in estimating earthquake magnitudes under difficult conditions.

Being a single-station approach, E3WS faces challenges in providing accurate location estimates, particularly in scenarios with low SNR. For location estimates in Murindó, the mean absolute error (MAE) for back-azimuth was 56.8 ◦ (Fig 4.5a), higher than the value (45.2 ◦ ) reported in Lara et al. (2023). This difference is likely due to the higher accuracy of back-azimuth estimates with increasing earthquake magnitudes, whereas Murindó primarily experiences smaller earthquakes. Similarly, in Cauca (Fig 4.5b), the reduced signal quality led to significant uncertainties in both distance and depth estimates. The back-azimuth errors in Cauca were especially pronounced, indicating that low SNR disrupted signal polarization, which is crucial for accurate back-azimuth estimation in E3WS. Similarly, for depth estimates, they are less accurate compared to the original E3WS results.

Although this experiment did not involve continuous data from the entire study period (2016-2023), continuous application of E3WS could further enrich seismic catalogs by detecting additional low-magnitude events within swarms. In the next section, we apply E3WS to a 12-year continuous dataset from Ecuador, providing a unique opportunity to asses the evolution of the seismicity during a very long period during which only one station was available all the time.

4.3 Characterizing the seismicity during a multi-year long period in Ecuador

This section presents preliminary results on ongoing work in collaboration with Quentin Bletery and Jean-Mathieu Nocquet , which aims to evluate the evolution of seismicity during long time periods in Ecuador, specifically in the La Plata region, through the application of E3WS.

Ecuador, located along the tectonically active northern Andes, experiences complex seismic activity driven by the interaction between the Nazca and South American plates. This subduction zone produces diverse seismic events, from large megathrust earthquakes to slow slip events (SSEs) - a type of transient aseismic fault slip deteceted by geodesy - and frequent seismic swarms (Fig. 4.7). The region's seismic profile includes notable historical earthquakes, such as the 1906 megathrust event (Mw 8.8), which ruptured a major section of the subduction interface. Seismic swarms and SSEs, particularly near La Plata Island, have long highlighted the intricate interplay between seismic and aseismic processes (Villegas-Lanza et al., 2016b). While these swarms are less destructive than megathrust events, their clustering behavior and interaction with slow slip complicate monitoring efforts (Vallée et al., 2013).

We apply E3WS to 8 years of continuous waveforms recorded at the Salinas (SALI) station, with the objective of building a long-term evaluation of the seismicity insensitive to changes in the number of available stations. The fault portion beneath La Plata island is known to produce SSEs, and a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) station, deployed in La Plata for an extended period, provides valuable long-term complementary observations. By utilizing E3WS, we avoid the observational bias introduced by stations deployed at later dates, ensuring a consistent assessment of the seismic activity over time.

E3WS detections reveal substantial seismic activity, with a total of 4,056 earthquake detections recorded between February 2013 and the end of 2020, based on data from the SALI station (Fig. 4.8). We compare the obtained seismicity evolution to an estimate of the moment release rate derived from GNSS records, which is an independent observation sensitive to aseismic fault slip (Nocquet, 2023). The GNSS-derived moment rate shows notable spikes, typically associated with mainshock-aftershock sequences, as evidenced by higher magnitude estimates from E3WS. Interestingly, the moment rate also rises during some seismic swarms, indicating that these swarms are detectable through GNSS measurements alongside E3WS. A close-up examination of 2013 shows clusters of E3WS detections that align with patterns characteristic of seismic swarms. The magnitude estimates from E3WS during this period are relatively low, confirming these detections as swarms rather than isolated large earthquakes. The preliminary results highlight that E3WS has successfully detected clear seismic swarms in Ecuador's subduction zone, many of which had not been identified in prior studies using multi-station approaches, such as the recent deep learning-based analysis by Wickham-Piotrowski et al. (2024).

To provide a clearer view of E3WS detections, we focus on the year 2013. In 2013, most E3WS distance estimates are around 160 km from the SALI station (see color scale in Fig. 4.9), aligning with the area known to produce seismic swarms near La Plata (Fig. 4.7). We observe a well-defined group of clustered detections based on SALI data, highlighting periods of concentrated seismic activity (Fig. 4.9). We detail the types of clusters detected by E3WS in Table 4.1. One group represents classical mainshock-aftershock sequences. Another group is composed of swarms induced by surface waves generated by teleseismic earthquakes. The last group is made of swarms detected at times of high moment rate inferred from GNSS suggesting a triggering by slow-slip events.

We find that most clusters are associated with the passage of surface waves following teleseismic earthquakes. For instance, Fig. 4.10 (Cluster 4) coincides with the passage of surface waves following the Mw 8.0 Solomon Islands earthquake, which occurred on 2013-02-06 at 01:12:25 UTC, as reported by the USGS. The surface waves lasted approximately three hours, as observed from the ISPT station, located in La Plata island (Fig. 4.10). Subsequently, throughout the day, E3WS detected 14 earthquakes with magnitudes mostly around magnitude 3.8. Filtering the waveforms to 1-7 Hz and 10-45 Hz, we verify that the events are real (Fig. 4.10) and that the algorithm is not triggered by the surface waves themselves. Similar observations Time have been made worldwide (Peng et al., 2011). We interpret this observation as indicative of an SSE triggered near La Plata by teleseismic surface waves (Itaba and Ando, 2011), pushing small asperities to failure and producing 1-to-3-hour long seismic swarms.

We find that Clusters 8 and 14 coincide with spikes in moment rate release derived from GNSS data (Fig. 4.9). More precisely, increases in the moment rate precede periods of heightened seismic activity, evidenced by a dense series of detections recorded by E3WS. This pattern suggests that SSEs trigger seismic swarms, providing insights into the relationship between aseismic slip and clustered seismic activity, that we will further investigate in future work.

4.4 Analysis of the foreshock sequence preceding the 2024 Arequipa earthquake (Peru)

This section presents preliminary results on ongoing work in collaboration with Quentin Bletery , Jean-Paul Ampuero , Anthony Lomax , Adolfo Inza , and Hernando Tavera , which aims to study foreshock sequence preceding the Mw 7.0 Arequipa earthquake on June 28, 2024.

The Arequipa region in southern Peru lies within a highly active seismic zone, influenced by the convergent boundary between the Nazca and South American plates. This tectonic interaction has historically led to large-magnitude earthquakes, posing substantial seismic risks for the densely populated areas nearby, including the city of Arequipa. Since early 2024, the Peruvian EEWS (SASPe), through E3WS, has consistently detected an average of one earthquake per day in Arequipa. However, the detection rate surged significantly following a M 6.3 foreshock on June 16, 2024, reaching 12 events per day (Fig. 4.11). During the two-week period leading up to the mainshock (M 7.0) on June 28, 2024, E3WS detected a total of 86 foreshocks with magnitudes larger than 3.

Time To analyze the foreshock sequence in greater detail, we first used E3WS to independently detect events on each of the closest stations near the sources, including SASPe stations SCVN, TNKA, SATQ, and the broadband YCA0 station, which is part of the Peruvian national seismic network. In this non-real-time application, E3WS operated continuously, using a 10-second sliding window with a stride of 1 second to detect seismic events. Once an event was detected, 46 seconds of P-wave data were used for source characterization, as rapidity is not required in this application. Due to limitations in back-azimuth estimates from single-station data, we combined E3WS detections with the Non-Linear Location (NLL) algorithm (Lomax et al., 2000, 2009; Lomax and Savvaidis, 2022) to refine earthquake locations.

Figure 4.11 - Number of earthquakes detected by E3WS per day in the Arequipa region from early 2024 to August 2024. Each point represents the daily count of detected earthquakes by the E3WS algorithm, with the color bar indicating the maximum magnitude detected in that day. The dashed purple line marks the M 6.3 foreshock on June 16, 2024, and the red dashed line marks the M 7.0 mainshock on June 28, 2024.

We apply the NLL algorithm to refine earthquake hypocenters by addressing the limitations associated with using only a few stations, which were all located on one side of the source region. Without Source-Specific Station Terms (SSST) corrections, the resulting locations can be highly sensitive to potential biases in the picks. In this analysis, the probability density functions (PDFs) from NLL results indicate that the epicentral constraints are most reliable along a NW-SE axis (approximately N55W - N125E), which runs parallel to the coastline (Fig. 4.12a). This orientation suggests the importance of comparing event locations along this axis, where epicentral uncertainties are minimized. However, in the perpendicular direction, there is a notable trade-off between epicentral and depth constraints due to poor resolution, which causes smearing along the S-P time arcs (Fig. 4.12b).

Figure 4.12 - Non-Linear Location (NLL) algorithm results showing earthquake probability density functions for detected seismic events in the Arequipa region. (a) The PDFs highlight that epicentral constraints are most reliable along a NW-SE axis (approximately N55W N125E), parallel to the coastline. This orientation reflects stronger accuracy along this axis due to the station distribution. (b) The perpendicular axis exhibits a trade-off between epicentral and depth constraints, as shown by the smearing along the S-P time arcs, resulting from limited depth resolution and the absence of Source-Specific Station Terms (SSST) corrections. White triangles indicate the locations of the stations used in the analysis.

The NLL method sensitivity underscores the necessity of obtaining comprehensive station data. Additional picks, especially from more distant stations, could help improve the depth constraints by reducing the depth-epicenter trade-off. Incorporating all available picks would provide more robust estimates of relative depths and contribute to a more accurate interpretation of the aftershock sequence. We are currently working to acquire additional data to refine SSST corrections, which will account for site-specific travel time anomalies and further enhance the precision of earthquake location estimates, leading to more reliable aftershock sequence analysis. Preliminary results suggest a predominant northward migration of foreshocks leading up to the mainshock (Fig. 4.13), which will need to be confirmed with more precise locations to be obtained with more data.

Conclusions & Perspectives

Conclusions

Wedesigned E3WS - the first fully AI-based Earthquake Early Warning System - to rapidly detect earthquakes and estimate their magnitude and location (Lara et al., 2023). E3WS has proven its effectiveness across various tectonic settings worldwide, establishing its reliability for real-time earthquake warnings. By integrating event detection, P-phase picking, and source characterization, the system provides quick and accurate estimates of earthquake magnitude and location, starting from the first three seconds of P-wave data from a single station.

We implemented E3WS as the core algorithm of the Peruvian earthquake early warning system (SASPe), which will soon issue public alerts, benefiting 18 million people (Lara et al., 2024). Additionally, we used E3WS for non-real-time applications, such as seismic swarm detection and characterization or aftershock forecasting. This flexibility allows E3WS to contribute not only to immediate earthquake early warning systems but also to longer-term seismic research.

E3WS has demonstrated its versatility in various seismic contexts around the world, including Peru, Japan, Ecuador, Colombia, Haiti, and other countries. The system's scalability and robustness allow it to be applied in both developed and developing regions, proving its effectiveness for seismic early warning purposes even in areas with limited infrastructure. Additionally, E3WS can be implemented on low-cost sensors, as demonstrated in Haiti (Calais et al., 2022), further emphasizing its potential for widespread adoption in resource-constrained settings.

E3WS offers the flexibility to operate with multiple stations, enhancing its ability to improve the accuracy of location estimates. In real-time applications such as the Peruvian EEWS (SASPe), E3WS uses data from multiple stations to refine its location estimates. For nonreal-time applications, E3WS can be integrated with the Non-Linear Location (NLL) algorithm or other algorithms to relocate seismic events more precisely, allowing for detailed post-event analysis, such as foreshock and aftershock sequence characterization.

Perspectives

The future development of E3WS holds exciting opportunities for advancing both seismic monitoring and earthquake early warning systems. Several key perspectives include:

Incorporating synthetic data: synthetic data can be integrated into E3WS for training, allowing tests to determine if magnitude and location estimates improve. Simulated seismic events can serve as a valuable tool to enhance the system's performance, particularly in undermonitored regions.

Expanding E3WS globally using low-cost sensors: E3WS has already demonstrated success with low-cost sensors, such as in Haiti. This scalability can be expanded globally by using affordable sensors such as Raspberry Shake, making it possible to provide seismic monitoring in regions with limited infrastructure.

Experimenting with temporary station deployments: E3WS could be deployed in regions where seismic monitoring is limited by installing temporary single stations to detect seismic activity. These temporary installations could provide essential data in remote or inaccessible areas.

Testing E3WS in extraterrestrial seismic contexts: The adaptability of E3WS can also be explored in extraterrestrial environments. Testing the system in new seismic contexts, such as the Moon or Mars, presents a unique opportunity.

## Abstract

Earthquake Early Warning Systems (EEWS) are designed to provide alerts before the most damaging seismic waves of an earthquake reach populated areas, giving people precious seconds to take protective actions. However, traditional EEWS rely heavily on dense seismic networks and often face challenges in rapidly detecting earthquakes in regions with limited infrastructure or fewer stations. In response to these limitations, and in order to provide faster warning even in well-instrumented areas, we design an AI-based algorithm, coined E3WS for Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System, which detects earthquakes and estimate their magnitude and location using 3 seconds of data recorded on a single station. This design not only improves the time response but also enables E3WS to operate effectively in areas with fewer stations, making it a flexible solution that can be applied not only in the studied regions but also globally, enhancing early warning capabilities in diverse tectonic settings. We install E3WS as the core algorithm of the Peruvian EEWS (SASPe for Sistema de Alerta Sísmica Perúano), providing timely alerts for subduction earthquakes along the coast and benefiting more than 18 million Peruvians. SASPe operates through a network of 111 stations, where E3WS is independently implemented. Beyond Peru, we use E3WS to forecast aftershocks in Haiti, to detect seismic swarms in Ecuador, and to study a foreshock sequence leading up to a major earthquake that occurred in Arequipa, Peru.

Keywords : Earthquakes, Early Warning, Artificial intelligence.

## Résumé

Les systèmes d'alerte précoce des tremblements de terre (EEWS) sont conçus pour fournir des alertes avant que les ondes sismiques les plus destructrices d'un séisme n'atteignent les zones peuplées, offrant ainsi quelques précieuses secondes aux populations pour prendre des mesures de protection. Cependant, les EEWS traditionnels dépendent fortement de réseaux sismiques denses et rencontrent souvent des difficultés à détecter rapidement les séismes dans les régions disposant d'une infrastructure limitée ou de moins de stations. En réponse à ces limitations, et afin de fournir des alertes plus rapides même dans les zones bien équipées, nous avons conçu un algorithme basé sur l'intelligence artificielle, nommé E3WS (Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System), qui détecte les tremblements de terre et estime leur magnitude et leur localisation en utilisant 3 secondes de données enregistrées sur une seule station. Ce concept permet non seulement d'améliorer le temps de réponse, mais aussi de faire fonctionner E3WS de manière efficace dans des zones disposant de moins de stations, en faisant une solution flexible pouvant être appliquée non seulement dans les régions étudiées, mais également à l'échelle mondiale, renforçant ainsi les capacités d'alerte précoce dans des contextes tectoniques divers. Nous avons installé E3WS comme algorithme central du système d'alerte précoce sismique péruvien (SASPe pour Sistema de Alerta Sísmica Peruano), fournissant des alertes précoces pour les séismes de subduction le long de la côte et bénéficiant à plus de 18 millions de Péruviens. SASPe fonctionne à travers un réseau de 111 stations, où E3WS est implémenté de manière indépendante. Au-delà du Pérou, nous utilisons E3WS pour prévoir les répliques en Haïti, détecter les essaims sismiques en Équateur, et étudier une séquence de séismes précurseurs précédant un séisme majeur survenu à Arequipa, au Pérou.

Mots-clés : Tremblements de terre, Alerte précoce, Intelligence artificielle.

## General Introduction

Earthquakes are among the most unpredictable and destructive natural disasters, posing a significant threat to human life and infrastructure. Over the past decades, several major earthquakes have resulted in substantial loss of life and extensive damage. For instance, the 2010 Haiti earthquake, with a moment magnitude (Mw) of 7.0, caused around 300,000 deaths and left 1.5 million people homeless. Similarly, the 2011 Tohoku earthquake in Japan, which had a Mw of 9.1, led to around 15,641 deaths and caused $211 billion in damages, making it the costliest natural disaster in history. These events highlight the critical need for effective and timely earthquake detection and response systems.

Earthquake Early Warning Systems (EEWS) are designed to detect the initial, less-destructive P-waves of an earthquake and provide alerts before the more destructive S-waves arrive. The development of these systems has proven to be a vital tool in reducing the impact of earthquakes by allowing individuals and automated systems to take precautionary actions. EEWS provide critical seconds of warning, giving people the opportunity to take protective measures and enabling automated systems, such as shutting down trains and industrial machinery, to prevent further damage.

Countries such as Japan, Mexico, and the United States have implemented sophisticated EEWS that send public alerts to populations in seismically active regions. Japan's EEWS, for example, has been instrumental in minimizing the impact of earthquakes by providing early warnings through mobile phones, television, and radio broadcasts. Similarly, Mexico's Sistema de Alerta Sísmico Mexicano (SASMEX) has been alerting the public to seismic threats since 1993, significantly reducing casualties in urban areas. However, while these systems are effective, their performance depends on the density and coverage of seismic networks, and the accuracy and speed of the underlying algorithms used to process seismic data.

Traditional earthquake detection methods rely heavily on networks of seismometers and algorithms such as the Short-Term Average/Long-Term Average (STA/LTA) method, which is used to detect seismic activity by identifying sudden increases in signal amplitude. While these methods have been successful, they face several limitations. For instance, sparse seismic networks in certain regions delay detection times, and algorithms such as STA/LTA can struggle in environments with low signal-to-noise ratios, leading to false positives or missed events. These issues highlight the need for improved detection technologies that can provide faster and more accurate warnings.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a transformative tool in seismology, offering new methods to enhance the detection and characterization of seismic events. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms are particularly well-suited for analyzing large datasets, identifying patterns, and making rapid decisions without the need for extensive manual intervention. These techniques have already been applied in a variety of fields, including healthcare and astrophysics, and their potential in seismology is becoming increasingly evident. In particular, AI models are capable of automating the detection of earthquakes, estimating their magnitudes, and providing timely alerts based on real-time data.

AI models have several advantages over traditional methods. Deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are capable of automatically extracting meaningful features from raw seismic data, reducing the need for manual feature engineering. These models can process continuous seismic waveforms, detect microseismicity, and identify patterns that may be difficult to discern using traditional methods.

Traditional machine learning models, such as XGBoost (XGB), offer a balance between accuracy, speed, and computational efficiency, making them ideal for real-time earthquake detection. A key advantage of these models is that they can be installed on simpler, lower-cost devices, such as Raspberry Pi, enabling their deployment in regions with limited infrastructure or directly onsite. This on-site processing approach significantly reduces the need for transmitting large amounts of seismic data in real time. For instance, in an Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) context, only small-sized warning information, such as estimated magnitude and location, needs to be transferred to the warning center rather than the entire waveform data. This makes the communication lighter, faster, and more robust, ensuring that critical alerts can be transmitted swiftly while minimizing bandwidth and reducing potential delays. Such efficiency is crucial in delivering timely warnings to vulnerable populations.

The integration of machine learning into earthquake detection reflects the ongoing need for faster and more reliable EEWS, especially in areas where infrastructure is limited, or people live in close proximity to seismic sources. Machine learning has emerged as a transformative tool in seismology, capable of enhancing the accuracy and speed of detection, as well as supporting new applications such as real-time magnitude estimation and source characterization. These advancements have the potential to significantly improve the effectiveness of EEWS, ensuring that alerts are delivered more quickly and accurately to populations at risk, allowing for better preparation and mitigation of earthquake impacts.

## Research Objectives and Thesis Structure

The goal of this thesis is to design and apply in a real-world context an ensemble machine learning algorithm based on a single station that functions as a complete EEWS package, capable of earthquake detection and source characterization estimates. The system should be compatible with both high-end and low-end sensors, allowing it to serve as both an EEWS and a tool for traditional tasks such as catalog generation (earthquake detection), P-phase arrival estimation, magnitude estimation, and determining epicentral distance, back-azimuth and hypocentral

This research seeks to bridge the gap between conventional seismological techniques and AI, offering a new paradigm for seismic hazard mitigation.

This thesis is organized into the following chapters:

- -Chapter I: Earthquake Early Warning: challenges and perspective - This chapter describes a broad overview of the seismic risks faced by human societies and the urgent need for enhanced detection systems. It begins by discussing the unpredictable nature of earthquakes and the crucial role of EEWS in reducing their impact. The chapter highlights the limitations of traditional seismological signal detection, especially in regions with sparse seismic networks, and the challenges posed by noisy environments. A key focus is placed on the development of scalable, single-station algorithms as a solution to these limitations. By leveraging Artificial Intelligence, single-station approaches can offer real-time earthquake detection and source characterization without the need for large sensor networks. The chapter emphasizes how these AI-driven models, particularly traditional ML algorithms such as XGBoost (XGB), can be deployed in cost-effective, on-site systems to deliver rapid and reliable earthquake warnings, even in areas with limited infrastructure, setting the stage for the thesis's focus on advancing EEWS through single-station AI algorithms.
- -Chapter II: Earthquake Early Warning Starting From 3 s of Records on a Single Station With Machine Learning - This chapter provides a detailed description of the Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System (E3WS), an EEWS that starts from 3 seconds of records on a single station, leveraging machine learning algorithms (Lara et al., 2023). It covers the system's design, which integrates detection, P-phase picking, and source characterization for magnitude, epicentral distance, depth, and back-azimuth estimation. The chapter also discusses the versatility and scalability of E3WS, along with its application to both minor and major earthquakes worldwide. Moreover, it presents a comparison with other EEWS systems, evaluating its performance and highlighting the feasibility of installing E3WS on low-cost devices, such as Raspberry Pi. This chapter serves as the foundation of the thesis, outlining the algorithm's design for application in Chapters 3 and 4.
- -Chapter III: Implementation of the Peruvian Earthquake Early Warning System -This chapter details the implementation and operation of the Peruvian Earthquake Early Warning System (Sistema de Alerta Sísmica Peruano, SASPe), which uses the Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System (E3WS) algorithm to issue real-time warnings for subduction earthquakes along the Peruvian coast (Lara et al., 2024). It describes the system's infrastructure, consisting of 111 strong-motion stations equipped with three-component accelerometers and low-cost processors, such as Raspberry Pi 4, enabling efficient on-site data processing. This chapter also presents real-time case studies of major earthquakes, demonstrating SASPe's performance and early warning capabilities. The scalability and potential for global deployment of SASPe are also explored.
- -Chapter IV: E3WS for seismic monitoring in different sparsely-instrumented contexts - This chapter highlights the application of the E3WS in various seismically active

regions, demonstrating its versatility in aftershock forecasting, foreshock analysis, and seismic swarm detection. In Haiti, E3WS was used to forecast aftershocks following the 2021 (Mw) 7.2 Nippes earthquake using a single low-cost sensor part of the citizen-based seismic network (Calais et al., 2022). In Colombia, E3WS was used to characterize the Murindó and Cauca seismic clusters. Additionally, this chapter discusses ongoing applications in Arequipa, Peru, where E3WS has been deployed to gain insights into the foreshock sequence leading up to the mainshock. In Ecuador, E3WS is currently being used to detect seismic swarms with data from the La Plata and Salinas stations, offering new perspectives on the behavior of seismic events in these areas.

- -Conclusions & Perspectives - This concluding chapter summarizes the main achievement of this PhD, which is the development and implementation of the Ensemble Earthquake Early Warning System (E3WS). E3WS, a machine learning-based system, is capable of detecting seismic events within three seconds using data from a single station, providing rapid and accurate early warnings. Its successful application across various seismic contexts, including its deployment in Peru and other regions with sparse seismic networks, demonstrates its effectiveness in offering quick estimates of earthquake magnitude and location. It also discusses potential improvements in the accuracy of earthquake detection and source characterization estimates, with an emphasis on refining the system's performance. The chapter also explores the potential for applying E3WS in different contexts, and outlines future directions for enhancing the system's capabilities in varied environments.

This thesis contributes to the field of seismology by providing advanced AI-driven solutions, particularly through Ensemble ML, for real-time earthquake detection and early warning. By enhancing the speed, accuracy, and scalability of single-station EEWS, the research has significant implications for global public safety and disaster risk reduction. The development of E3WS and its implementation in the Peruvian EEWS mark the revival of single-sensor EEWS. Moreover, its successful application in Haiti demonstrates the potential of AI to improve seismic detection in regions with limited infrastructure. These advances pave the way for the next generation of earthquake early warning systems, with the potential to save lives and minimize economic damage in future seismic events.

## 1.1 The earthquake threat and the benefit of early detection

Natural disasters have long posed significant threats to human societies, with earthquakes standing out as one of the most unpredictable and destructive forces of nature. Over the past two decades, earthquakes have resulted in substantial loss of life and displacement of millions. For instance, the 2010 Haiti earthquake, which struck with a moment magnitude (Mw) of 7.0, caused approximately 300,000 deaths and left 1.5 million people homeless (DesRoches et al., 2011). Economically, the consequences can be equally devastating. The 2011 Tohoku earthquake and subsequent tsunami in Japan, which resulted in the deaths of around 15,641 people (Mori et al., 2011), caused an estimated $211 billion in damages, making it the costliest natural disaster in recorded history (Kajitani et al., 2013).

According to the NCEI/WDS Global Significant Earthquake Database 1 , since 2000, an average of 35,568 people died annually from earthquakes, with economic losses averaging $77,191 million per year (Figure 1.1). The sharp contrast between the 2010 Mw 7.0 Haiti earthquake and the 2011 Mw 9.1 Tohoku earthquake highlights the crucial role of early earthquake detection. Despite the Tohoku earthquake's larger magnitude, its offshore location and Japan's advanced Earthquake Early Warning System (EEWS) helped mitigate the death toll, as many fatalities were caused by the tsunami rather than the earthquake itself. Japan's EEWS provided residents with precious seconds to brace for impact, automatically halting trains and issuing alerts through mobile and broadcast systems. In contrast, the 2004 Mw 9.1 Sumatra earthquake, which triggered the devastating Indian Ocean tsunami and caused over 283,000 deaths, saw catastrophic losses across several countries due to the absence of a regional EEWS (Lay et al., 2005). The absence of an EEWS left the population completely unprepared, reflecting the critical importance of rapid earthquake detection and early warning systems in saving lives, especially in densely populated or high-risk areas.

Moreover, the economic impact of earthquakes extends far beyond the immediate cost of damaged infrastructure. These disasters can disrupt entire economies, leading to long-term financial losses that hinder development, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. For instance, the twin earthquakes in Turkey on February 6, 2023, with Mw of 7.8 and 7.6, caused over 45,000 deaths (Dal Zilio and Ampuero, 2023) and an estimated $34.2 billion in infrastructure damage, equivalent to 4% of the country's 2021 Gross Domestic Product (GDP). However, the total recovery cost is likely to be even higher due to the broader economic disruptions that follow such events (Kahraman, 2023). The aftermath of these disasters places significant strain on national resources, diverting funds from essential services like education and healthcare, and further exacerbating poverty and inequality.

Effective detection can play a crucial role in minimizing the economic and infrastructural damage that often accompanies these disasters. According to the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), earthquakes events have been responsible for 58% of all deaths (721,318) caused by natural disasters over the past two decades (Figure 1.2), highlighting the deadly nature of these events and the urgent need for reliable detection and warning systems (Van Loenhout et al., 2020).

Recognizing the importance of earthquake detection, the international community has emphasized it as a crucial element of disaster risk management strategies. The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, adopted by the United Nations in 2015, underscores the need for enhanced monitoring and early warning systems to reduce disaster risk and strengthen resilience (Pearson and Pelling, 2015). This global commitment reflects the understanding that early detection and warning are key to minimizing the impacts of earthquakes and ensuring that communities are better prepared to respond and recover.

The functionality of an EEWS consists of detecting the initial seismic waves (P-waves) and issuing real-time alerts, estimating the earthquake's location, magnitude, and potential impact before the more destructive secondary waves (S-waves) arrive (Figure 1.3). Typically, these alerts are issued based on an alert radius determined by the estimate of Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) or Peak Ground Velocity (PGV) thresholds (Zollo et al., 2009). These systems provide crucial seconds to minutes for individuals and automated systems to respond, prompting protective actions like the 'Drop, Cover, and Hold On', which has been shown to reduce injuries and fatalities (Burkett et al., 2014). Automated responses, such as halting trains, shutting down power plants, and activating emergency services, further prevent damage. By leveraging the near-instantaneous speed of light communication, EEWS transmit warnings faster than seismic waves travel, allowing alerts to reach affected populations before the arrival of the more destructive S-waves and surface waves. This brief but critical window of warning plays a key role in saving lives, reducing economic losses, and enhancing the resilience of critical infrastructure. Expanding and improving EEWS, especially in seismically vulnerable regions, is crucial for effective disaster preparedness and response.
